items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: Why, when New Zealand taxpayers already fork out $2.9 million
to support netball and $3 million for rugby, must they then pay again to watch their
national teams in both world cups?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The member is simply wrong. New Zealanders can watch it for
free on Prime and they can watch it live at a number of venues.

items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: Given that the Prime Minister wants to see the silver fern on the
flag, why has he not already allowed New Zealanders to see our Silver Ferns for free on
our State-owned TV for the Netball World Cup?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: New Zealanders can see it for free on free-to-air television.
Energy Sector—Energy in New Zealand 2015
9. BRETT HUDSON (National)  to the Minister of Energy and Resources : What
recent reports has he received on energy trends and growth in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Yesterday the
annual review of the energy sector, Energy in New Zealand 2015, was released. It
shows that in 2014 renewable energy made up near ly 40 percent of New Zealand’s total
primary energy supply. This is a record high and places us third in the world behind
only Iceland and Norway. Also in 2014 renewable electricity generation hit just under
80 percent, the highest level since 1996. These are fantastic results, showing that we are
making real gains, transitioning to a lower carbon energy future, and making the most
of our country’s renewable advantage.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: What insights does Energy in New Zealand 2015 reveal about
resource development last year?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Energy in New Zealand 2015—the report that I have been
referring to—shows that oil and gas exploration was up in 2014, with over $2 billion
spent here by operators; the highest ever level of expenditure in this country. This is a
great result and shows that the Government’s approach to encouraging exploration and
development is a real success. Energy diversity is the key to achieving energy security,
affordability, and sustainability, whi ch is why we take a long- term view, with a mixed
and a balanced approach, pursuing opportunities in both renewable and non- renewable
energy.
5800 Oral Questions  13 Aug 2015
Overseas Investment—Outcomes of Overseas Ownership of New Zealand Land
10. STUART NASH (Labour —Napier) to the Minister for Land Information :
Has she received information from the Overseas Investment Office which confirms the
statement of the Minister of Economic Development that “We have not been as
effective as other countries in ensuring that overseas investment into New Zealand has
provided the additional benefits”?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I agree with the
Minister for Economic Development’s statement that there has been lower overseas
investment in comparable countries, and there will be many things that we can learn
from how those countries are attracting overseas investment. However, any application
for sensitive land that comes through the Overseas Investment Office must provide
examples of substantial and identifiable benefits to New Zealand. The Overseas
Investment Act strikes an important balance between ensuring sensitive New Zealand
assets are adequately protected while facilitating foreign investment that provides
benefits to New Zealand. We cannot be Fortress New Zealand if we want an economy
that is internationally competitive and better placed to deliver higher incomes and better
services to New Zealand.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Can she confirm that since the start of 2012 to the end of 2014 the
Overseas Investment Office has approved 296 consents for the sale of sensitive land to
foreign investors and turned down exactly zero?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I am not going to confirm the exact statistics that the
member has discerned, but what I would say is to explain that there is a process for the
receipt of Overseas Investment Office applications. Not all of them are then put forward
for assessment. So there is a pre -assessment process that ensures only high -quality
applications are considered. Once accepted for assessment, applications go through a
rigorous assessment process as the Overseas Investment Office assesses the applications
against the criteria. In recent times, three have been declined.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: I would like to table a document that shows since the beginning—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I know what it will show. We just need the source of the
document.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: The Parliamentary Library.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No. That is available to all members.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: How many jobs have been created by the 716 successful foreign
investors in sensitive New Zealand land who promised to create jobs as part of their
consent application, or does the Overseas Investment Office not keep statistics on this?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Each individual application is considered according to the
criteria that are set out in the Overseas Investment Act. Actually, this side of the House
strengthened those requirements in 2010 with the ministerial directive. In addition to
that, in 2012 the High Court counterfactual test ensured that New Zealand receives
benefits.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You probably know what it is
about. It is a very clear question. How many jobs—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I think the way forward is for the question to be repeated for
the benefit of the Minister.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Sure, I am happy to do that. How many jobs have been created by the
716 successful foreign investors in sensitive New Zealand land who promised to create
jobs as part of their consent application, or does the Overseas Invest ment Office not
keep statistics on this?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Although the Overseas Investment Office does not
aggregate data on the lists of benefits successful applications will have for New
13 Aug 2015 Oral Questions  5801
Zealand, every single application has to show  measurable and identifiable benefits to
New Zealand. This includes the number of jobs.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: What is the value of increased export receipts promised by the 358
successful overseas investors in sensitive New Zealand land who promised t o increase
export receipts as part of their consent application, or does the Overseas Investment
Office not keep statistics on this?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I am more than happy to take the House’s time going
through some of the answers that  have already been provided to that member through
written questions. As I said before, the Overseas Investment Office does not aggregate
data. There is an assessment on every individual application to make sure that any
approvals provide benefits, whether that is exports or jobs, to New Zealand.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: In light of those answers, why does this Government not think that it is
important or seem to care about the value, or lack of it, created by the sale of New
Zealand farmland to foreign investors?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I did make it very clear in my opening answer to the first
question that there is a high test, and we have also said that in the ministerial directive
letter we put tougher measures in place. There is an imp ortant balance here that this
Government is very conscious about. Foreign investment is vital to New Zealand, as
Minister Joyce pointed out in his earlier answer today, but, equally, in terms of any
approvals of any sensitive assets, including land, New Ze alanders want us to make sure
that there are substantial and identifiable benefits for them.
Benefits—Sanctions and Impact on Children
11. JAN LOGIE (Green) to the Minister for Social Development: What actions, if
any, has the Ministry of Social Development taken to ensure the well -being of children
in families subjected to benefit sanctions, given that sanctions of sole parents have
increased by 19.98 percent in the last year?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I am not sure where
that member is getting her figures from, or her maths, but they certainly do not match
any of the figures that I have received  from the Ministry of Social Development. Sole
parents are expected to be available for and looking for work, to care for their children,
and to keep Work and Income updated on their progress. Beneficiaries receive a number
of notifications before a sancti on is even put in place. Beneficiaries with children can
never be sanctioned for more than 50 percent of their main benefit, and they continue to
receive the full amount of any supplementary assistance. In fact, under this Government
fewer people are having their benefit stopped because of sanctions, and there has been a
34 percent reduction in suspensions and cancellations since 2011.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This was a question on notice that
was authenticated in the response to—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! It is quite appropriate for a Minister to
then dispute the figures that the member has provided as authentication for that question
to be accepted—quite acceptable.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: So w hat, if anything, is the Minister doing to address the fact that two -
thirds of sanctions have been for missing one appointment, which then halves a family’s
income, throwing children’s lives into chaos as parents struggle to pay for rent and
power?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Well, in fact, that is not true. That is not correct, and there is
no way that a sanction of that nature would be applied for missing one appointment. In
fact, the member is correct that the most common reason for a sanction is missing
appointments, but it is not too difficult to expect people to turn up for a pre -arranged
5802 Oral Questions  13 Aug 2015
appointment. If they cannot make it, Work and Income people do go out and meet
people in their own homes. A telephone call will actually avoid any further action.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Does the Minister believe children’s warmth and security of housing
should ever be put at risk due to their parent missing an appointment because Work and
Income had not processed their paperwork, they missed a bus, or there was a death in
their family?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: What I can assure that member is that if any of those issues
are raised with Work and Income by the applicant, they will be taken into account.
Work and Income is there to support those solo parents and to make sure that their
children get the very best start they could possibly get in life.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Who wants to go first?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: It is pretty clear from the question that the Minister was asked
whether she believes a child should ever be put at risk—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just have the point of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: —and that was not addressed in her answer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member is referring to the last supplementary question that
was asked, it was very clearly addressed. The member took the opportunity of quoting
three reasons why a sanction may be imposed, and the Minister took the opportunity of
saying that if Work and Income knew of those three reasons, it would not impose the
sanction. The question has definitely been addressed. [ Interruption] Order! If the
member wants to stay and continue her line of questioning, she had better adhere to the
Standing Orders.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Is the Minister still hoping to achieve her Better Public Services target of
a 25 percent reduction in the number of people receiving a main benefit, des pite the
stormy economy ahead, by making life so stressful and precarious that people are
coming off benefits even if they have no job to move into?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This Government is determined to ensure that all New
Zealanders have the opportunity to live full and successful lives. That includes people
who are reliant on a benefit, and the children in those homes. We know that the best
way out of poverty for those parents and children is through work. So we are definitely
focused on achieving that 25 percent reduction and helping those people live better
lives.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Why is the Minister intent on holding the line that getting people off a
benefit will improve child poverty, when the household income survey released today
shows that despite a drop in the number of children in beneficiary households there are
now an additional 45,000 New Zealand children living in poverty?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I would absolutely dispute the last statement that that
member made. It is a gross and serious misrepresentation of the report that was released
today.
Primary Sector—Agricultural Compounds and Veterinary Medicines Amendment
Bill
12. TODD BARCLAY (National —Clutha-Southland) to the Minister for Food

items.speaker: Safety
items.text: What announcements has the Government made that will help our primary
sector have greater access to the latest technologies and agricultural products?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: This week the Agricultural
Compounds and Veterinary Medicines Amendment Bill was introduced to the House.
The bill will increase the data protection period for companies registering in novative
agricultural products. It means that our primary sector will have better access to the new
13 Aug 2015 Oral Questions  5803
products that it needs in order to manage plant and animal pests and to keep farm
animals healthy.

items.speaker: Todd Barclay
items.text: How will this bill increase  New Zealand’s access to agricultural
products?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: The New Zealand market is a small one, and suppliers need
time to recover their product development costs before their data can be accessed by
competitors. This bill will enco urage overseas suppliers to register new products, while
still allowing for robust competition in the New Zealand market place.
Solid Energy—Voluntary Administration

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from Richard Prosser, the Hon Clayton
Cosgrove, and Gareth Hughes seeking to debate under Standing Order 389 the
announcement today that Solid Energy has been placed in voluntary administration.
This is a particular case of recent occurren ce involving ministerial responsibility. The
announcement makes it clear that Solid Energy has been placed into temporary
voluntary administration and that in the meantime it will continue to operate normally
under its existing board of directors. It has been reported that there are no plans for
redundancies during the period of administration. Although being placed in voluntary
administration is significant, the longer-term outcome of that decision is not yet known.
The business of the House should not be  set aside just because an announcement has
been made, even though it may be important. There must be such an element of urgency
that the matter must take precedence over other business. In this instance, I am not
persuaded that there is an element of urgency that warrants the setting aside of the
business of the House. The application is, therefore, declined.
In Committee
Debate resumed from 11 August on the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill.
Social Development and Housing Sector (continued)

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The Chamber is in Committee for
consideration of the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill. Members, when we were
last progressing the estimates debate we were debating the votes for the social
development and housing sector —volume B.5 and volume 10—Vote Building and
Housing and Vote Social Development. Poto Williams had the call and she has 1 minute
remaining.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: Just to round off my last call, I
want to say that the estimates debate is all about transparency, it is all about openness,
and it is all about accountability. In the case of moving over $15 million from the
Christchurch Housing Accord for affordable housing without telling the people of
Christchurch, or even its own partner, the Christchurch City Council, this fails to meet
any test of accountability.
I would ask the Minister for Building and Housing to come to the Chamber and tell
us why he chose to do  that without suitable notification to not even the people of
Christchurch or the Christchurch City Council. This fails to meet any test of
accountability, of transparency, or of openness, and I suggest that the Minister be held
to account for that.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Last night Philippa Howden -Chapman
and Graeme Beattie spoke at the Speaker’s Science Forum about their respective
research on housing and health. Their point was to talk with MPs about the evidence on
5804 Estimates Debate 13 Aug 2015
which we as a community of MPs could build both cost -effective and health -effective
policy in housing. This is an issue that was dealt with by the Social Services Committee
in looking at the estimates and there has been  some Budget provision for some part of
some policy around home insulation, but it is weak and will not prove to be as effective
as it could be because this Government simply will not prioritise this level of evidence -
based policy detail. We have seen toda y in the 2015 report on household incomes more
evidence about the state of housing for families, which should be driving urgency in this
policy.
In general, the information presented last night was not particularly new to MPs.
New Zealand homes are poorly built—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Mr Chair?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No—sorry. The people behind you
should know better. Thank you—keep going.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. New Zealand homes are poorly built for
our climate and for the use of families. They are damp and they are cold, and this
means, of course, that families spend an excessive amount on their power bills and too
many, especially the elderly and children, get sick from the effects of this poor housing.
According to the evidence, Warm Up New Zealand, the home insulation programme of
the Greens and Labour, and then the Greens and National, has a cost -benefit ratio for
grown-ups of nearly 4:1 and, for children, a cost -benefit ratio of 6:1, showing that there
is enormous economic value in investing and warming up with good insulation and
good heating in New Zealand homes for grown -ups and for kids. And yet we are still in
the situation, the evidence shows, where 1,600 New Zealanders die each winter. We
have 1,600 winter -related deaths —avoidable, housing -related deaths —every year. We
have 1,600 people dead because of poor housing—that is wha t the evidence that was
presented last night showed—and a very large proportion of them are of children.
We all know what the solutions are, and the evidence showed us that again last night.
First, improve the building standards on insulation, heating, and ventilation to remove
condensation and improve heat retention. Secondly, require rental properties to have
and meet a set of warrant of fitness criteria to improve the safety of those homes. The
study last night showed that there was a nearly 40 percent reduction in injuries based on
home modifications and, subsequently, there was a significant decrease in the cost of
ACC, which is a major cost to all of us. Thirdly, provide home insulation and heating
subsidies to increase take -up across all households —not a select few but across all
households. The evidence of that shows that hospitalisations fell by 27 percent in the
first 12 months, and by 61 percent for the most intensive insulation and heating
interventions. These are three straightforward, well -known, well-costed, well-thought-
out policies that are well- understood, and the evidence shows that they would be very,
very effective.
The household income report that came out today shows that the number of low -
income families with excessive housing costs r emain at a historic high —50 percent of
people getting the accommodation supplement are paying more than 50 percent of their
income in housing. Of those families in households that reported major problems with
dampness and mould, 70 percent were on the lowe st incomes, so the lowest -income
families are the most likely to suffer from the poor quality of New Zealand homes. And,
of course, the evidence from this report today shows that housing is increasingly
expensive, degraded, and unsafe for New Zealand families.
At the dinner last night one MP noted that “Surely, if MPs in the House knew that
1,600 people die a year from poor housing - related illnesses, we would be up in arms
and do everything that we could to fix it.”, but the fact is that we do know this. We have
13 Aug 2015 Estimates Debate 5805
known this for years, and, no, there is not an urgent drive to fix New Zealand’s housing
quality. There is no urgent drive to increase the home insulation and heating subsidies,
or to make sure that there is a warrant of fitness for rental properties.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Thank you
for the opportunity to contribute to this estimates debate. I want to add to the debate an
element of the measures that the Government is currently taking to support students. I
am going to do so at a time when we are hearing quite a lot of deba te about what
students do with the money that the Government sends their way for support of their
tertiary education. So I would like to talk a little bit about my responsibilities within the
social development portfolio for student loans.
We have made ch anges to the student support. It has allowed us to free up money
that we can invest in improving the quality of the tertiary education we provide. Back in
2011 we passed legislation to make sure benefit and student allowances increase every
year along with inflation. That lines up very nicely with the same changes that we made
to give some certainty for increases to other welfare payments as well. Interestingly,
that was not an action taken by the previous Labour Government, along with its partner-
in-arms at the time, the Green Party.
Each year the rates and thresholds for a range of Work and Income assistance and
StudyLink assistance will rise to keep up with increasing living costs, and back on 1
April this year we saw the annual general adjustment go up by 0.51 percent, which of
course was indexed at the time. So we are supporting students. We are retaining the
student loan repayment threshold at $19,084 until April 2017, and increasing the student
allowance rates for families with children by $25 a week,  which will kick in on 1 April
next year. We are retaining the student allowance parental income threshold at
There is another thing that we are doing for students. Let us face it, a lot of what we
hear about students is that they are time poor —they are very busy studying. They are
very busy in many cases with some part -time work to support their study. This year
more than 130,000 students have benefited from the improvements that we have made
to student loan and allowance application processes . These make it easier in the
following ways. They allow for a pre -filled online application process, which saves
about 30 minutes for every student getting on there. The one other thing that does is it
saves money for the taxpayer, because the taxpayer is  not spending more time with
these students, getting the answers from these students in order to fill in the necessary
forms to apply for things. So, in fact, we are in that same way getting better bang for the
buck for our taxpayers as well. There is also a digital repository called Connect, which
allows students and parents to scan the necessary documents, the evidence that they
need to apply to StudyLink.
You know, there are some amazing statistics that demonstrate how well this is going.
Unanswered cal ls have been slashed from 800,000 unanswered calls back in 2013 to
fewer than 8,000 this year. That means, again, a saving for the taxpayer because there is
a 22.5 percent drop in foot traffic at the StudyLink offices. So this is yet another
example of thi s Government being careful with the money that the taxpayers are
entrusting to us. It has been said in the Chamber this afternoon—and I am going to say
it again because we cannot say it often enough—that the way for families to help
themselves if they are dependent on a welfare benefit is, wherever possible, for the
Government to assist them into work. That is how their children, their lives, their health,
and their welfare, indeed, are bettered. Therefore, this Government is going to many
lengths—extreme lengths in some cases—to assist families to benefit from having work
and having an income coming into their household.
5806 Estimates Debate 13 Aug 2015
We have heard sanctions debated here today, and it is reprehensible to hear members
of this Committee misrepresent the obligations we pla ce on people and the way that
sanctions are applied. We know at the heart of this that if sanctions are applied, that
means quite a drop in income. That is never done without good cause, and if there are
reasons for that person to have failed an appointment, then all they have to do is say so.
But we also know that having an excuse repeatedly, time after time after time again,
might indicate an inability to really show commitment towards going to appointments,
to undertaking training, and therefore no commitment to bettering their own lives.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Earlier in this estimates debate we talked
about the Prime Minister’s cynical comment that Auckland homeowners are happy
about becoming wealthier because of skyrocketing house prices. It is so clear from those
comments that that is the reason why this Gov ernment has done nothing substantive or
serious about the Auckland housing crisis. All we get are public relations -  driven half
measures. We talked about the spectacular failure of Nick Smith over the last few years
to do anything about increasing the supply of housing in Auckland, to the extent that the
housing shortage is getting worse to the tune of 5,000 houses every year and the
Productivity Commission is projecting a shortfall of 60,000 by 2020.
But there is so much more to talk about in the housing  area. After the Government
has denied for years that the rampant property speculation in Auckland has anything to
do with the fact that house prices are going up on average by $500 a day, we saw just
before the recent Budget what this Government so often does: deny, deny, deny there is
a problem, and when the focus groups start to show up a bit of public concern, it wheels
out a grudging half measure. And that is exactly what the Budget announcement on the
so-called 2-year test and the brightline test, to try to catch a few speculators, is.
That policy is basically like hunting speculators with a very small butterfly net, and
John Shewan, one of the Government’s most respected tax advisers, came out within
days of that announcement to say it will not do an ything to rein in house prices in
Auckland, and it certainly will not catch very many property speculators. Meanwhile,
this Government is completely at sea on the question of a foreign buyers’ register. We
have had four different statements —from the Prime Minister, from Nick Smith, from
Louise Upston, and from Steven Joyce —all saying different things. In fact, I think that
Louise Upston was the most candid. She said that it is not a foreign buyers’ register, it
will not be public, and it will not tell us th e information that is needed for this debate.
Well, I say good on the Minister for at least being candid with the public, because I
cannot say the same for her colleagues.
This Government is completely in denial about the effect of property speculators,
including offshore money, in the Auckland housing market. It is totally in denial about
it, in spite of the fact— amazingly, for the Government —that the polls say that in the
order of 70 percent of New Zealanders want to see a register of foreign buyers. It is
good enough for David Cameron, who is saying that a fully accessible and searchable
register of foreign property buyers is a priority for his Government in the United
Kingdom. It is good enough for David Cameron, and it is good enough for the centre -
right Federal Government in Australia, which has the same policy. But this Government
will not go near it. All it has done is promise a very weak, very diluted attempt to gather
a little bit of data on foreign buyers. It is completely in denial.
The Australi an policy, which also happens to be the New Zealand Labour Party
policy, is a ban on foreign buyers buying existing houses. Foreign buyers are currently
responsible for channelling billions of dollars of investment from China into new builds.
Apartments in Sydney and Melbourne are being put up like there is no tomorrow, and
they are almost all funded by offshore money. That policy of a ban on foreign buyers is
a sensible policy that is working. Steven Joyce has been going around saying that it is
13 Aug 2015 Estimates Debate 5807
not working and that it has been a failure. He has been flatly contradicted by experts in
Australia who have said that, actually, the Federal Government in Australia is
completely committed to the policy and is toughening it up. In the state of Victoria they
are jailing foreign buyers who rort the rules. Meanwhile, this Government denies it is
even a problem.
Let us talk about another aspect of housing policy. I want to say what an excellent
speech it was by Metiria Turei about warm, dry homes. All I want to add, re ally, is that
the Government’s announcement in this area was yet another grudging half measure.
The public want to see mandatory standards for rental accommodation to make sure
they are warm and dry. They want to see insulation standards. They want to see heating
standards. But what does Nick Smith do? He allows landlords, who have avoided taking
advantage of the generous taxpayer subsidy for the last few years, a 4- year grace period
and very weak standards.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Earlier in this estimates debate the
Labour member Poto Williams made a comment and a statement, and asked a question:
“How do people in Canterbury feel about that?”. Well, I can tell you how they feel
about that. This National Government won the party vote in every electorate in
Christchurch and every electorate in Canterbury. The reason was that they believed in
us and they trusted us. The first chance we have had to repay them for that trust and that
belief is this Budget 2015, the Budget that is working for New Zealand. Budget 2015 is
working for Canterbury. Budget 2015 is working for my electorate of Waimakariri.
The member Phil Twyford spoke about Housing New Zealand. Well, she needs to
get out of he r office and go and talk to Housing New Zealand. I went to Housing New
Zealand to listen to its update on rebuilding and repairing 5,000 houses and 700 homes.
There was no Opposition member of Parliament at that event. They had not even
bothered to turn up. I have listened to the appropriations around social housing and I
have met with those at Housing New Zealand. It is great to hear that in “Waimak” we
will end up with more Housing New Zealand houses post -earthquake than we had pre -
earthquake.
In this debate on Vote Building and Housing and Vote Social Development we heard
from Darroch Ball. Unfortunately for him and New Zealand First, he could not talk
about social housing. The reason was that New Zealand First voted down the social
housing reforms and t hose social housing appropriations that will give an extra 3,500
New Zealanders access to social housing. Those social housing appropriations and
social housing reform will give extra wraparound services to vulnerable Kiwis, giving
them support around ment al health, giving them support about alcohol and drugs, and
giving them support in education, training, and employment. That is why he could not
talk about the social housing appropriation. Also New Zealand First could not talk about
the appropriation for children in hardship, because it voted down that as well —a
package that will give Working for Families an extra $12 a week through that
appropriation. It is an appropriation that will give beneficiary families up to $25 a week.
New Zealand First members vo ted that down. They are not putting New Zealand first;
they are putting themselves first. Can I congratulate this Government on its
appropriations and targeted investment, because what we know through allocative
efficiency is that if we put money in, we can get better results out.
I would like to take some time to talk about our youth services. What we know
around that social investment approach is that if we put $1 in, we will get $2.53 out
through reduced future liability. That is what this Budget is about. We know that Vote
Social Development 2015 is one of the biggest expenditures in this vote at about 25
percent, at about $25 billion. It is right that this Government is taking a social
investment approach. We know that with the Youth Service we are put ting $1 in and
5808 Estimates Debate 13 Aug 2015
getting $2.53 out. This is a group of vulnerable New Zealanders: 38 percent of them are
victims of domestic violence, 76 percent of them have been victims of emotional
neglect, and 5 percent of them have been homeless and victims of sexual a buse. So it is
right with this appropriation that we are investing in services that are making a
difference in New Zealanders’ lives. That is what this Government is doing. We are
listening to New Zealanders. We are working hard for them. We are the party for the
working people. If we look at youth services, we know through research that 86.5
percent of participants are engaged in education, training, and employment. When we
are talking about Vote Social Development 2015 the reason we can invest $25 billion is
that we have a got a strong economy, we have got strong economic management—

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: This House does know the seriousness of
the problem with housing quality and affordability in this country. This House also
knows that 1,600 people die every winter in this country because of poor -quality
housing. MPs in this House have heard me ask questions of Bill English about one of
those 1,600, Emma -Lita Bourne, a baby who di ed last year from housing -related
illnesses. So it is impossible to say that we do not know, and we do not know what to
do. We do know, and we do know what to do. Although the politicians, particularly the
Government Ministers, are ignoring the evidence and even the faces of the people who
are affected by poor -quality housing, the ministerial officials do seem to be taking it
into account.
I want to identify two areas where the officials have been listening to the evidence
and putting to the Ministers solu tions to help these kids and help these families. Here is
one solution they proposed before the Budget: an integrated healthy homes service for
families of children with housing -related health risks —this is from the Government’s
own ministerial papers; this is from Treasury to the Prime Minister —like Emma -Lita
had. It was a $2 million a year fund—not very much money —for 3,000 children who
have already been admitted to hospital for respiratory and infectious diseases. These
children, the officials say, can b e identified as being at risk of serious health problems
like rheumatic fever. It was a $2 million fund for 3,000 identifiable sick kids, and what
does the Government do? It said: “No, it is not in the Budget.” No, it’s not a solution
that it is prepared to consider. Then we have people like Anne Tolley saying that
children’s health and well-being is the Government’s priority. Well, where is the plan to
deal with the threat to children’s health from poor housing? Where are the Children’s
Teams that are head ing out to these families’ homes to insulate, ventilate, and put in
place good heating?  Why are these 3,000 identifiable babies not worth this
Government’s attention and a measly $2 million a year? When did these kids’ lives
suddenly become optional?

items.speaker: Here is another example
items.text: assistance with winter energy costs. It is in the Treasury
paper to the Prime Minister, Bill English, and other Ministers. It is assistance with
winter energy costs called the “winter warm -up payment” of $300 a year, going to the
parents of children with a child aged under 1. It would be a great start for a low -income
family with a little baby to get a winter warm- up payment to help them to pay for their
winter power bill. It is about $4 million a year —a bit bigger than the other one. W hat
did the Government say to that option? “No—big ‘X’. No, we are not going to provide
low-income families with little babies just a little bit of extra money to help them get
through this winter.” The Government could have done it —the officials said that it was
possible to do it this year —but it decided not to do it. There is no justification for the
Government saying that it cannot do anything about these 1,600 deaths, about the babies
who are getting sick and being hospitalised, or the babies who never come home—no
excuse at all. It has the money, it has the policy, and it has the officials who support it. It
13 Aug 2015 Estimates Debate 5809
could roll it out under existing services, and it chooses not to. We can never accept a
Government that is prepared to put the lives of babies at risk like this for nothing.
There is not even any ideological reason for it to say no to this. What is wrong with
the Ministers that we have in place? They cannot look at genuine proposals or ways to
help the most vulnerable families and the sickest babies , to make sure that we have
fewer babies getting sick, fewer babies going to hospital, and maybe more babies at
least coming home. The families that these options were directed towards are seeing
their babies going into hospital and they are not coming out . Where is the Government
in making sure that these families have what they need? The Government will make a
claim about the $25 in increased benefits, but everyone knows that the families will be
lucky if they get to see $20 of that. It does not come in until next year, and it is a farce.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: It is nice to be here. I want to respond to
some of the comments by the previous Labour speaker, Phil Twyford. He was correct in
identifying that there is a trade -off in the Budget; in fact, trade -offs are inherent in
Budgets. When that money is spent on housing, one of the key parameters that
determines how much benefit can be provided to the citizens of New Zealand at the
expense of taxpayers is the underlying cost of housing. Housing is the block in the cost
structure for the Government’s provision of social housing.
We have to accept —and I think it was lost on the previous speaker, Metiria Turei —
that there is an element of scarcity in this. The question is: how do we expand the
overall amount of resource available for New Zealanders to consume? That is why there
is no point in simply deciding that a foreign buyers’ register and knowing who owns the
homes in some nominal sense is going to increase the overall amount of economic
resource available in New Zealand to be consumed.
Denis O’Rourke: It’ll help. It’ll help.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: It is fundamentally flawed to believe that that could help, as
the member is trying to say.
In truth, and the really dirty reality of that register, is that what it seeks to do is
identify the ethnicity and the nationality of the person who owns the beneficial interest
in a piece of property. That is the reality of what the New Zealand First members’
register—their dirty little secret—attempts to do. They don’t like it up ’em, but that is
the truth, and it was a disgraceful political move to make.
They then say, in a related sense, that the limit in the availability of housing that we
are going to spend on in this Budget is due to so -called speculation. Well, the fact is we
know that the level of speculation is inversely proportional to the elasticity of  supply of
housing. It all comes back—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: So do something about it, then.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: —we will come to that, Mr Twyford —to the amount of
resource available to be spent.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: You’re supporting a Government that’s done nothing.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: But as Mr Twyford truly knows —he truly knows, with all his
feigned outrage and anger —that the real issue is the regulatory environment and the
supply of buildable land. And he goes  on and on with publicity stunts. He goes on and
on, trying to blame this person, that person, and the other, and saying that a tax will
help, even though it has not helped in any other jurisdiction, and nobody has ever built a
house in order to pay more t ax. What he is unable to bring himself to do is to reach
across the aisle and be constructive.
You see, people on this side of the Chamber know that the Resource Management
Act is one of the greatest constraints on the supply of housing and therefore puts
pressure on this Budget. People on this side of the Chamber would like to reform it and
increase that elasticity of supply to address the concerns raised by Mr Twyford.
5810 Estimates Debate 13 Aug 2015

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: You’ve had 7 years and you’ve done nothing.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: If he objects to 7 years, what about the previous 9? He could
fix this problem. If he had any magnanimity and if he had any maturity, he could reach
across the aisle and say: “Here is a set of Resource Management Act reforms the Labour
Party will support.” But have we seen anything like that in this Chamber ever?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Yes, we have.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: No, we have not. The problem is that the ones that he would
like to support —and he knows it —would be completel y impotent and ineffectual
because they are asinine.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Read my press release, David.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Here we have it: policy making from the Labour Party comes
down to a press release. The fact of the matter is that the kind of Resource Management
Act reform that would increase the elasticity of supply of housing, that would solve the
problems with registers being called for and with speculation, and that would actually
increase the amount of economic resource available to be allocated in this Budget would
mean changing the fundamental principles of the Act.
It would mean changing the principle sections, sections 5, 6, and 7. That is what it
means. It means taking a Resource Management Act that has 156 mentions of
inappropriate subdivision and reducing that number. But will the Labour Party reach
across the aisle and support substantial Resource Management Act reform? I think if it
was prepared to do that, we could actually solve a big problem for all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: David, you’re an idiot. Don’t embarrass yourself.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. The member just said
that you are an idiot, bringing the Chair into the debate. I think that is quite
inappropriate.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I did not hear him, but the member’s
time has now expired.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I welcome the
challenge from David Seymour to the Labour Party to reach across the Chamber to try
to find concord on the Resource Management Act, because he is too late; we have
already done it. Labour has repeatedl y told National and the other parties in
Government that we would be more than happy to work with them on the Resource
Management Act, but the National Government keeps saying: “No. It’s our way or the
highway. No, Labour, we’re not prepared to work with y ou.” So thank you, David
Seymour, for reiterating the challenge to the Labour Party, because we are more than
welcoming of it. I want to hear the same challenge made to the National Government, to
encourage it to reach across the Chamber and work in a cros s-party manner with parties
of the Opposition, so that we can actually deal with some of the real issues in the
Resource Management Act —some of which do, indeed, relate to housing. We would
welcome that challenge. We would love to have that, so good on David Seymour for
laying down the challenge. At least he does something useful when he actually shows
up in the Chamber.
I want to talk about what is really happening on the ground with housing for people,
because there is a lot of rhetoric being spouted in here. The Government is trying to tell
us the various plans and initiatives that it has got, but I want to talk about the real
experience of people in my electorate of Palmerston North. The real experience in
Palmerston North is that where there used to be State houses, there is now acres and
acres of empty land, and some of that land has remained empty for years. Finally, after
7 years in some cases, the Government does have a plan for that land. The plan is to sell
it off. That would be fine if the plan wa s to use the money from the sale of those houses
to build more houses in Palmerston North, but that is not the plan at all. The
13 Aug 2015 Estimates Debate 5811

items.speaker: Government has been quite clear about this
items.text: it is reducing the number of State houses. It
is reducing the provision of social housing in Palmerston North, just as it is doing in
regions right across the country. So that is a fact. That is what is actually happening if
we cut through the rhetoric —if we cut through all the noise. We just have to look
around us in our own communities, especially those of us who live in the regions, to see
that, actually, National’s plan is to reduce the provision of State and social housing.
National members argue that there is actually no need for social housing. Well, if
they genuinely believe that there is no need for it, I have a recommendation for them: go
along to your local Salvation Army, go along to your local Women’s Refuge, go along
and talk to any number of the organisations that represent people with disabilities and
ask them whether there is a need for social housing —because the answer will be
resoundingly: “Oh, yes. Yes, we are desperately short of housing for people who are the
most vulnerable—the people who are in need.” What is happening as a result of this is
that Work and Income is now telling people to go and see the Salvation Army because
they cannot get on to the waiting list for a State house—the Salvation Army that has had
to get rid of its women’s hostel in Palmerston North because of a lack of funding
because it lost contracts w ith the Government and whose men’s hostel is now under
extreme pressure and has been taking people whom it is probably not fit to take, which,
because the Salvation Army does not get the appropriate funding from the Government
to house those people adequately, has been raising the ire of the people who live around
that men’s hostel.
Women’s Refuge has had to close one of its facilities because it has lost funding
from the Government, and it is now having people referred to it by Work and Income.
Any woman with children who goes to Work and Income and tries to get on the
Housing New Zealand list and is denied is told to go to Women’s Refuge whether or not
they actually qualify for the services that Women’s Refuge provides. Women’s Refuge
is there to provide s upport for women who are trying to escape domestic violence. So
now Women’s Refuge is having to waste its own resources screening women in order to
determine whether or not they actually fit its criteria. Work and Income cannot do its
job properly and actu ally ensure that those people who are in need are able to get
supportive accommodation. That is the real thing. Whatever the Government tells us —
whatever spin and lines it has for us —those are the facts. That is what is really
happening in our regions.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: I realise that the time is about to expire on this debate,
but I just want to get in a few quick points before this debate does conclude. This is the
end of the Committee of the whole House stage on the appropriations. We are focusing
on the social aspects of them today. I still want to reiterate, at the end of this, that this
Budget that provided these appropriations, provided these estimates of what is going to
be spent over the ne xt little while, will be transformational for New Zealand. It will be
transformational for those people who are the most vulnerable in New Zealand. For the
first time in so many years —so many years —families who are on benefits and who
have children living in their homes are going to see a rise in their benefits. It is this
Government that is bringing this into place.
It is this Government that is helping to support our teen parents. We saw some
legislation go through just the other day to extend the age for the young people who are
at a high risk of staying on benefits for long periods of time and also for teen parents.
What we know is that these people who find themselves in a position where they are on
a benefit, either as a teen parent or with other high -risk factors around them, will spend
on average up to 13 years on benefits. This Government is absolutely aspirational for
those people. It aspires to see them achieve so much more.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I move, That the New Zealand
Flag Referendums Bill be now read a third time. This bill will give New Zealanders the
opportunity, for the first time ever, to vote on the flag that represents them and their
country. We made a commitment as a Government, ahead of the last election, and this
bill delivers on that commitment for a referendum on the flag.
The first of two postal referendums will soon be held over a 3- week period from late
November and into December. I just remind the House about the process that was put in
place, of which this legislation is part. Early on the Government, with the assistance of a
cross-party group of MPs, set up the Flag Consideration Panel. It was resourced by the
Government, but in every other respect it has been operating independently and has
now, through a process of public engagement, particularly through its website, produced
a long list of 40 flags.
The members of the cross -party group took quite an interest in the legislation and
made a number of comments during the Committee stage, questioning whether officials
had acted properly in the advice that they gave to the  cross-party group. I just want to
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5813
put on the record that I have no concerns about the roles that officials have played.
Cabinet made a decision in October 2014 about the process and the budget for this
project. The decisions were announced publicly at the  time, and the Cabinet paper and
minute were made immediately available online. So the process has at all times stressed
the independence of the Flag Consideration Panel and the transparency of any decision
making around it. I want to thank the cross-party group for their contribution to this bill.
Consensus recommendations of the cross -party group are determining the planned
referendum dates, the preferential voting system used in the first referendum, the
number of alternative flags on the first referend um voting paper, and the approach to
regulating referendum advertising. The bill contains the measures required for the
referendum process to progress. This includes setting out the postal voting processes of
the two referendums and a promoter statement requirement for those who are publishing
referendum advertising. The bill also has measures for implementing the new flag if
voters decide to change the flag, and they are separate and parallel to the work the Flag
Consideration Panel has been operating.
The panel has now released a long list of alternative flag designs, and we look
forward to them accomplishing what must be a difficult task of selecting from those 40
flags four flags for the purposes of the first referendum. Now that the process for
underpinning the referendums —the passage of this bill—will be complete, I think that
the public debate over the flag is likely to rise a few notches in intensity but also in
relevance to what the flag is about. Up until now it has been dominated, to some extent
at least, by criticism about the amount of money that is being spent. There has been
quite a bit of expression of views by people who have every right to oppose any change
whatsoever and oppose the opportunity for the public to make a choice, which seems a
bit odd given that that opposition has come mainly from the most populist party in
Parliament, New Zealand First, which in every other respect believes we should have
referendums on everything. But apparently on this, when it comes to putting New
Zealand f irst, New Zealand First members do not believe that New Zealanders are
capable of exercising a choice about the flag. It is almost as bizarre as the Labour Party
position, which is to support a change in the flag but oppose a referendum and not vote
in it.
Clearly we are heading out of those swirling political waters, fortunately, to the
sunny uplands where New Zealanders will get to decide what kind of symbol they
regard stands best for their country and their own sense of identity. I look forward to a
robust debate in that respect, because, as the Flag Consideration Panel found out, there
is a wide range of associations that New Zealanders have between the name of their
country and their flag and the values that they think it represents. I would imagine t hat
the discussion about the choice of the flag will represent that wide range of associations.
And then there is the sheer difficulty of understanding the intuitive connections. If you
think New Zealand is about equality or fairness or freedom, what does that look like on
a flag? Of course, there will be extensive debate about the balance of representation of
our history, rich as it is, and our future, aspirational as that is.
In my capacity as a member of the House I want to acknowledge the role the Prim e
Minister has played in bringing about this legislation and, in fact, the referendum.
Leadership is always challenging, and there is no doubt that he has been challenged in
his desire to see this debate occur. But I have absolutely no doubt that in pushing this
issue forward he is showing the qualities of leadership and a fundamental belief that
New Zealanders should have this opportunity. The logic is pretty simple: New
Zealanders have gained in confidence about their economic capacity and about their
place in the world. It is a hard- won confidence, through various controversies and
5814 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
recessions and internal political debate, and there is a unique opportunity now for
people to choose how that confidence should be expressed.
The Prime Minister was, at the time he raised this issue, almost uniquely aware of the
need for that opportunity. But the debate that we will see from here, I think, will see
many New Zealanders grasp that opportunity with two hands and express their views. I
would counsel the Leader of the Opposition to change his position—he does not usually
have much difficulty in doing that —on not voting in the referendum. Even if he is
opposed to change, there is a fundamental legitimacy about a referendum as a way of
deciding it. Opting out seems to me to be the worst response to the challenge. Get in and
argue—have a different point of view, try to persuade others. But for a political leader
to say “Well, I’m not going to participate.” is actually letting down his party and letting
down his role.
I look forward to the expression of the will of the people even if the New Zealand
First Party fears it. I think it will be good for New Zealand to have this debate, and who
knows—if the alternative is good enough, many of us just might vote for it.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I want to start where the
Deputy Prime Minister nearly left off, and that is with the role of the Prime Minister in
this vanity project. I am an old- fashioned parliamentarian, and I think the role of the
Prime Minister is to stand up in this Parliament and to state his views. I waited through
the first reading of this legislation, I waited through the second reading of this
legislation, and I waited through the Committee stage for John Key to get on his feet
and to give his views. I was waiting for the Prime Minister to give his views as part of
this debate, and what did I see? He decided to contribute to this debate in the House by
way of Twitter. He got the timing wrong because he did not anticipate Solid Energy, but
he would not stand up on his hind legs in this Parliament and give his views. For a
Prime Minister of a country who has a pet project, it shows, to me, a lack of
commitment—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Thrown Bill under the bus

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: —no, I cannot say that —to a parliamentary
democracy.
I do want to make a few other points. I think what many members do not realise, and
what John Key certainly does not realise, is that this is a very serious matter for a lot of
people. It is not just, you know, “Shall we have five or six bottles of champagne with
our dinner at the barbie in Hawaii?”. It is not something like, you know, “Shall we buy
another Mercedes or another Porsche?”. It is a matter that is a symbol of New Zealand
and important to a lot of people. I think Twitter does make some pretty good
contributions in the area, and the one that I saw yesterday that likened changing the flag
to an individual getting a tattoo is something that is pretty accurate. It is something that
is a serious, long-lasting decision and one around which the process should be good and
where the timing is also important.
Over the last couple of years and the next few years the G overnment and
communities around New Zealand are spending over $100 million commemorating the
First World War. The symbol under which New Zealand soldiers fought and died was
the New Zealand flag. Their representatives, the RSA, had some very strong views —
one about the change, but in particular about the destruction or the possible destruction
of that symbol during that period of commemoration. Those representatives of the RSAs
around New Zealand were treated disgracefully by the Justice and Electoral Commi ttee,
which was considering this bill. Ten minutes was given to the national organisation to
be heard—10 minutes only. And what happened? Over the 3 weeks of adjournment —3
weeks of adjournment—Jacqui Dean refused to call the committee together to hear the
submissions and to give people more time to be heard. Jacqui Dean, assisted by Alfred
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5815
Ngaro, Jono Naylor, and Chris Bishop, denied 747 people who had made an application
to be heard by the select committee their ability —[Interruption] Now Jacqui Dean is
trying to blame Louise Upston. Sorry, I—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: You forgot about Louise—so mean.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, I do not think she was there on the day I was
there. So we will just leave it. The other ones were the nasty ones . They were
particularly nasty to the 747 mainly returned servicemen who used the Facebook page
circulated by the RSA to put their submission in—

items.speaker: Jono Naylor
items.text: By the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Well, yes—the Labour Party helped develop it. That is
right. [ Interruption] Members opposite laugh at returned soldiers because they used
Facebook to put in submissions.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: We’re laughing at Trevor Mallard.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: No, not via me —directly to the committee, Brett
Hudson; directly to the committee. They were not allowed to be heard, and those
members made that decision, and that is a disgrace. It is an absolute disgrace that that
member went on holiday for 3 weeks instead of convening the select committee during
the select committee sitting period.
I want to make a few other points —first of all, about the cross -party committee. I
have said previously that the Labour Party —and I will take responsibility because I
gave advice on the matter —made a mistake going into that process. We trusted the
National Party members when they said that they would be straightforward and above
board. And they were not. There were about three tasks. One of them involved giving
advice on the shape of the referendum. At the meeting that considered it, every single
party other than the National Party said that there should be a yes/no vote at the first
referendum. Every single party that was present there was of that view. The shape of the
referendum as recommended by the cross -party committee was rejected by the National
Government Cabinet, and that is a disgrace. The committee put forward a group of fine
New Zealanders as a suggested oversight group, and what happened? Some of the best
people—

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: Most of them got through.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Oh, most of them got through, but a group of them
were knocked out and replaced by National Party hacks —people like Julie Christie.
Julie Christie was respons ible for the part of the programme that spent $2,300 getting
people to meetings. For every single person who got to a meeting —the part that Julie
Christie was in charge of—$2,300 was spent to get each individual there. Rod Drury, of
course, was someone who—it is no secret—was agreed on by the wider committee. The
online campaign has been fantastic. The work of the chair has been, I think, highly
ethical given the very difficult task that he was given, but the confidence in the group
was destroyed by the fact that Cabinet rejected the nominations of the cross -party
group.
People have different views as to whether to vote or whether not to vote in the first
referendum. I have heard my leader say that he, basically, cannot be bothered and that
he will consider  it later. I actually have a different view. I used to think we should
change the flag. I think now is an inappropriate time to do it. I am going to pick the least
popular option—the one that I think is most likely to be rejected by the people of New
Zealand. I will put that at No. 1 and the one that is most likely to be accepted at No. 4,
because I think that is what I can do to reinforce the fact that this is not a time for
change.
And, as a final point, we are yet to get from Bill English the cost of the change
process if it goes forward and the cost to the Crown. Will it be $100 million, $200
5816 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
million, $300 million, or $400 million? How much is it going to cost the Crown? How
much is it going to cost to change every crest in the country? Every Government crest in
the country includes the flag, and in the part of the bill that says what the crest is, it says
“the New Zealand flag.” So all the crests have to be changed, and that does not include
private sector spending. This bill is a dog. It should be rejected. I know it is not going to
be, and, in a funny way, John Key losing is going to be fun.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is an honour to speak on this bill, the New
Zealand Flag Referendums Bill, but it is disappointing to see that a member who has
probably been here for over a hundred years and has served this Parliament for such a
long time—he has been here for many years —has come to a point where he knows and
he has agreed. In fact, at the Justice and Electoral Committee, he told us that he agrees
with the changing of the flag. It is in the Hansard. He said that changing the flag is
actually the right thing to do, yet today, in this House, openly to the public of New
Zealand, he is opposing the bill out of spite —only out of spite. He knows that it is the
right thing to do. He knows that it is the right thing to do, but he is choosing not to vote
for it out of spite. It is a sad day when a member who has been here for that long and
who has made a contr ibution can get to that point and, out of spite, vote against the
legislation.
That member also made comments about the 740 form submissions that wanted to
make an oral submission, and he has been going on about it in his all of his speeches,
even in the C ommittee stage. That member knows, because he has been here long
enough, that form submissions are taken as one submission and as a whole. He has sat
on select committees, he has been a backbencher, he has been chair of a select
committee, and he has been a Minister. That member knows that a form submission is
taken as one submission. So to get up here and tell us that we did not allow the
democratic right of 740 form submissions is not true and is not correct at all. Again, it is
an act of spite—an act of spite. Instead, we heard the submissions that came forward
from people who took the time to write their submissions and who took the time to say:
“Yes, I would like to come before the select committee and be able to present my
submission.”
In the speeches that we have heard on this flag referendums bill, we have heard
people talk about this possibly being a vanity bill for the Prime Minister. I want to sort
of contest this point. In fact, Carmel Sepuloni made this point just the other day when
she said that  the title of the legislation could be “The Prime Minister’s Vanity Bill”.
Well, let me just remind that member. In 1970 when the then National Minister of
Internal Affairs , Allan Highet, actually put a petition forward, was that vanity? No, it
was not, because he was challenging the fact that there should be change. In 1988
former Labour MP and Minister of Foreign Affairs Russell Marshall —and I know the
honourable member over there Trevor Mallard will probably know him —was that
vanity? Was it vanity when he said that there was a point of change that was needed? In
1989 the Listener  had a magazine article in which it actually had a competition, and
there were over 600 entries and seven finalists. The current flag of 1902 was the winner
only by a minority, a nd the people said: “Actually, this dispels the myth that this is the
time for change.” Was that vanity? No, it was not.
Let us get to February 1992, when the late Hon Matiu Rata, former Minister of Māori
Affairs for the Labour Government and the founder of Mana Māori Motuhake, called
for a redesign to re -establish a national flag. Was that a vanity project? No, it was not.
Why? Because even Mr Mallard knows that it was the right thing to do. This is what he
said; it is in the Hansard. He said: “Yes, the current flag of 1902 represents our history
and our heritage, but does it represent our future? No, it does not.” That was his
challenge.
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5817
Denis O’Rourke: It does—it does.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: At that point in time —and listen up, Mr O’Rourke —the RSA
had challenged and contested every single petition to change the flag. In 1992 the RSA
conceded and said this: “This will not go away. The issue of change is going to be
coming from one generation to the next.” [ Interruption] So they said this, Mr O’Rourke
and Mr Mark: “If there is to be a change, let it be by referendum.” In other words, let
the people choose—let the people choose —and that is exactly what this bill is about. It
is letting the people choose to have their day here.
We know that many people right up and down the country have turned round and
said that this is something we should look at. This is  what the bill is doing. It is saying:
“Let the people choose.” So what have we got here? We have had 10,290 alternative
designs—10,290 alternative designs have come forward— and 26,000 New Zealanders
have shared what they stand for. In other words, they ha ve been asked this question:
what are the values that are important to us if we were to redesign the flag? And I know
that Mr Mallard would say that that is the right process: let the people choose. What are
the values that are reflected in this flag? What is the narrative behind the design? That is
what has been asked of our people.
There were 2.7 million views of the flag gallery. That is what has happened. There
were more than 8,500 online visits and 6,000 visits to the workshops and information
stands. What does this say? In other words, the people are saying this: “Let us choose.
Let the people choose.” Mr Mallard knows that this is the right process. The members
of New Zealand First know that this is the right process. They are confused. As my
good fr iend Jono Naylor said, they are so confused that they have had to write it
down—in fact, I think they have squiggled it out now. On that little sticker, it said “New
Zealand—why?”, because even they were confused; they thought that it was an
Australian flag, right?
Denis O’Rourke: Nonsense.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I think Mr O’Rourke has got his little blue marker out and he
has squiggled it all out. That is right —he has taken it away. Even he knew that he was
confused about what that  flag was. So in order to allow that confusion to be dispelled
and in order for the nation to choose, we believe that this bill is the right bill. We are
simply saying this: let the people choose, as they have asked to do. As the RSA has
said, let it be by referendum.
My final point is about this talk about the fact that —it is like MMP —we went out
and asked the people this: do you want it or not? Let us remember that we had had years
of talk about MMP, so people understood it. You cannot ask people for a de cision on
something they do not know about. What we have asked people is this: let us put out the
designs; let us make sure that people have a view on what that alternative could look
like; let us know what the narrative is, not only about our history and our heritage but
also, as the late Matiu Rata said, in this place even, in front of Mr Mallard, “Let’s
choose a flag that represents our future.” That is what this referendum is doing, and the
people will choose that. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is not often that I
disagree with my good friend the member for Hutt South, Trevor Mallard.

items.speaker: Alastair Scott
items.text: Oh, yes, it is.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: No, no. You would be surprised, actually, on the other
side of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I get on with the right-wingers OK.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Oh, yes, we can take that up later, Mr Mallard. His
depiction of his thought process around the flag—he was a person who wanted to see it
change and then he has come to believe over time that it should stay the same —is not a
5818 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
position I agree with. I am one of the members of the Labour Party who thinks that
there is a place for a new flag for New Zealand, but I am equally a member of the New
Zealand public who is angry with John Key for turning a process—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: You’re always angry with John Key—doesn’t count.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: No, no. Jacqui Dean contributes meaningfully, yet again,
from the back row there. I, along with a lot of other New Zealanders, am angry with
John Key that a discussion about this and a discussion about our national identity ha s
become a vanity project for him. There is absolutely no doubt that that is what has
happened.
Ironically, as Mr Mallard says, the vanity does not extend to coming to Parliament to
actually talk about the flag change. But, in terms of the way this entire discussion has
now played out in the New Zealand public, it has played out as being about John Key
and his desperate desire for a legacy and his desperate desire to leave something here in
a flawed process that actually does not, as Alfred Ngaro would have  it, give New
Zealanders a say in the way that it should on this. A flawed process is the actual legacy
that John Key has left New Zealanders on this matter.
I have a feeling that two things are going to happen with this referendum. The first of
those—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Oh, yeah, you’ve got your crystal ball.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right, I have. I will see if Mr Mark agrees with
these. I have a feeling there are two things that are going to happen with this
referendum. The first of t hose is that the turnout in this referendum will be
disappointing. The turnout in this referendum will not reflect what the National Party
says to us is such a significant thing and a once in a lifetime opportunity. I think we will
find the turnout will be  low, in part because of matters that were discussed during the
Committee stages of the debate around the way that the referendum has been held, the
technology that has been used, and all of those things. So I think that is the first thing
that I would say.
The second is that I suspect that the ridiculous order in which this referendum is
taking place will come home to haunt National, because, by not asking New Zealanders
the question of whether or not they wanted to keep the flag first, it put in place a process
that will undermine National’s own argument, in my view. Government members are
not being straight up with New Zealanders. They are not going into this conversation
with New Zealanders saying: “Do you want this change?”. It has been raised in this
House several times before.
If you were to spend thousands and thousands of dollars driving all around the
countryside looking at different houses to try to decide whether or not you wanted to
buy a house, and you had not even worked out whether you had e nough money to do it,
how ridiculous would that be?

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: It’s going to cost more than $25 million.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Exactly. How ridiculous would that be? And that is the
problem with this process. The complete failure to t reat New Zealanders with respect
and actually look at this in a way that is a sensible and logical order is ridiculous.
The Labour Party in the Committee stages of the debate proposed two amendments.
The first of those was to defer the referendum for 5 ye ars. I think that was a sensible
suggestion. I agree with other Labour speakers that at this time in New Zealand’s
economic situation and in this time in New Zealand’s social situation, the time is right
to push that back. To my mind, I would like to see N ew Zealand have a conversation
about our identity and about our nationhood that encompasses not only a symbol like
the flag, which is important, but also the future of our constitutional arrangements.
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5819
To me that is the thing that John Key wants to avoid. He wants to avoid the
discussion about our overall constitutional arrangements, which should be happening at
the same time. I am deeply disappointed that it is the vanity of John Key rather than the
substantive issue of what kind of arrangements we should have in New Zealand. How
can we be having a conversation like this about our flag without the deeper conversation
about whether we are a republic, whether we are a constitutional monarchy—

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: What does sovereignty mean?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Yeah, exactly. As my colleague Nanaia Mahuta says, what
sovereignty means today in New Zealand, in the 21st century. But we are not having that
conversation, because the Prime Minister wants to diminish it and reduce it down to his
vanity project and his attempt at a legacy, because real leadership would be taking on
that bigger challenge. Real leadership would be saying: “Let’s engage all New
Zealanders in a conversation about how our country should be run and what values are
important to us and what arrangements reflect those values in our constitutional
arrangements.” But that is not what we have got. What we have got is an ill -thought-
out, two-stage referendum process that is round the wrong way.
The first of our considerations was to defer for 5 years to be able to take on some of
those ideas. The second proposal that we put forward was to cancel the second
referendum if 50 percent of eligible voters do not vote in the first. And this really is a
serious question: if the National Party really believe that the flag is this significant and
this important, why not adopt that? Why not adopt the idea that, actually, it is important
enough that at least half of New Zealanders have a say? But that was not  picked up, and
we know, from the debate in the Committee stages, that that is because National MPs
are just not confident. They are not confident that people will participate to that level.
It is time for the National Party to front up to New Zealanders and to stop being so
out of touch with what they must hearing in their electorates and around the country
about this flawed referendum process. That is actually, in my view, why John Key has
not participated in the debate, because he is worried about it. H e is worried that it is
going to go down and that it is going to tarnish “Brand Key”. Well, he should front up
to New Zealanders, and he should accept that at least 50 percent of them should
participate in the first referendum in order for the second one t o occur. Unfortunately,
both of those proposals by the Labour Party were rejected in the Committee stages.
I want to refer, just before I come towards the end of my contribution, to the select
committee process, because I think it does sum up what has gon e wrong here. For
committee members—and Alfred Ngaro did this when he stood up before —to say to
747 people, who were, as Trevor Mallard says, largely returned service people who got
together and decided that they want to put forward their views, and National members
of the committee outright rejected—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: 15,000 did it.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Yeah, but 747 on that page. But 747 wanted to be heard,
and were rejected on that side of the House. And, again, I ask: if they truly believe this
is significant and if they truly believe this is the big change that they want to do in terms
of national i dentity, how dare they not give those people the right to be heard? How
