dare they deny those people, who have got so much history with the flag, the right to be
heard? So I am deeply disappointed that we have reached this point.
As I said at the start of my contribution, I still believe that there is a place for a
change in the flag, but it comes as part of a wider process, and anything other than that
wider process of consideration of our future constitutional arrangements makes this
tokenism. It makes th is process a vanity project. It is a huge lost opportunity for New
Zealand to truly reflect on who we are in the 21 st century. Instead, we are subjected to a
5820 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
political process for John Key to be able to give his so- called legacy to New Zealand. I
think that is wrong, and that is why I oppose this bill.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Labour members have found themselves in
an invidious position over the consideration of this bill because they act ually want to
change the flag. And that is a problem for them because they campaigned on wanting to
change the flag—in fact, they campaigned on having a referendum to change the flag —
and they have found themselves wrong- footed, somewhat, by the fact that t his
Government, which also campaigned on changing the flag, has actually done what it
said it would do. Having found themselves wrong -footed over the process, they are
having to cast around for reasons to oppose the bill. It has been a little bit like danc ing
on the head of a pin because you raise one foot and you just about topple off. It has been
like that the whole way through this process. It seems to me that when the Labour
Opposition finds itself trying to advance an argument that it does not actually believe in,
it then starts attacking the process. That has been very apparent, also, throughout this
consideration of the flag bill.
I want to dwell a little bit on the select committee stage of this bill and talk about
how the Justice and Electoral Commi ttee made certain decisions about the hearing of
submissions. Those of us who are backbenchers and who spend a lot of time in
committee rooms will know that a committee will have a discussion at the start of the
process in order to decide those mundane thi ngs like time frames —how long we are
going to invite people to speak for; what the conditions are that they come in. When
committees are faced with some pragmatic decisions, which is what this committee did,
we make—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The member went on holiday. She didn’t sit during the recess
week. It’s an outrage. She voted not to sit during the recess week.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: They make those decisions as a committee. And so what happened
in the consideration of this bill—and, for those people sitting at home or listening on the
radio, they will hear a bit of noise in the background. That is Trevor Mallard. That is
Trevor Mallard losing the argument yet again, because Trevor Mallard has got no
argument to make, and so, in the  absence of any argument, he is making a lot of noise.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Some of the decisions that the committee made were about how
long we were going to invite people to speak for and about how many people we were
going to hear. It was a committee decision; it was not a National Government decision.
In fact, was it not the Green Party that voted with the Government on this? Yes, it did.
So the ma jority of the committee voted that it would consider as form submissions a
number of submissions coming into the committee.
Form submissions are a normal part of select committee practice, and it does surprise
me that the Assistant Speaker of the House, wh o is also the person making the most
noise over this and who should know his Standing Orders, does not know his Standing
Orders, or does not purport to know his Standing Orders, in this case. Normal select
committee practice is that the committee can decid e to group as form submissions a
number of similar or identical submissions, treat them as if they were a petition, and
consider them in that way. That is what the committee decided to do.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The member never read them.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Trevor Mallard is making that noise again because he is losing the
argument again.
I just want to go into those form submissions a little bit more because the question
then becomes: “How did those submissions come to the committ ee?”. Well, it might
surprise some members of the public to know that those submissions came to the
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5821
committee via the Labour Party website. Those form submissions came to the
committee via the Labour Party website, where submitters clicked on to the Labour
Party website and were given a tick box to tick. So all that people had to do—and they
were having their say, absolutely —was say: “No, I disagree.” Well, that is fine, but
when you get a whole lot of those submissions, with the same people making absolute ly
the same point—and it would have been a sizable pile —I would contend that grouping
them together with a sample on the top that reflects everything that lay beneath should
be treated as a form submission.
So when Trevor Mallard gets to this House —and every time he does, he loses the
argument just a little bit more —what he is doing is he is wilfully ignoring what he
should know about parliamentary process. I will tell the House about the select
committee—and, at this point, I want to thank the members for their consideration of
this bill—it was a lively debate, as a select committee debate should be. We heard very
carefully the submissions that were made to the committee, and we made a couple of
changes as a result of our select committee consideration.
I am not going to make a terribly long contribution to this debate. I think that this bill
is relatively simple. It sets out the framework by which New Zealanders can have a say
on whether or not they wish to change the flag. The final point that I want to ma ke
about the process and about some of the Opposition contributions —mostly in the name
of Trevor Mallard—as they lose the debate, is that this is not about the select committee
process, actually. This is not about what the Prime Minister may or may not have had in
his heart when he generated this debate, although we are pretty sure that it was in the
best interests of New Zealand. It is not about that, actually. What this is about is
enabling New Zealanders to have their say on what represents them by way of a flag.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: With this third reading we the representatives
of the New Zealand people have delivered ourselves of our collective wisdom on the
issue of the New Zealand flag debate. We are about to conclude our part of the exercise.
We have been voting and will, no doubt, vote again—today, perhaps —by 63 to 58, to
proceed with the two referendums on the basis of the piece of legislation that is in front
of us.
We have expended a quantum of hot air on this issue on both sides of the House on
behalf of the people we represent. The 63 members who are about to support the
legislation have argued that the original idea was a good one, that the dual process for
the national decision is appropriate, that the cross-party panel is legitimately empowered
to decide the four options, and that the expenditure is worthwhile.
The 58 members about to oppose the legislation have argued different things. New
Zealand First opposes the fundamental idea of any change to the New Zealand flag. The
people should not be offered a choice. Labour supported the idea of potential change,
but, although many members among them cheerfully indicated they would support a
new flag, they rejected the process and proposed a different one. Individual members of
that party have felt the need to convey to the public their personal views.
We in the Green Party maintain that changing the flag is in itself an insufficiently
important constitutional thing to be pursued by itself alone. It is, we have said,
essentially a matter of optics and not worth proceeding wit h unless it were accompanied
by other far-reaching constitutional reform.
In the first reading I identified the inconsistencies, as we saw them, on the part of the
Prime Minister in personally proposing the process for a change of flag. He claimed
there w as a mandate for change, offered an unsolicited personal view in favour of
change, and then acknowledged there was a need for a public debate and that there was
no presumption of change. So the public could be forgiven for being a trifle confused.
With all of this flying around on both sides of the debate it is no surprise that party
5822 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
politics has subsumed the substantive issue of the debate, following the Canadians half
a century later and altering —should we decide as a people to do so—the emblem of
who we are and what we stand for.
Meanwhile the panel has worked with professionalism and the designers have
worked with creativity and passion. We have some 40 options and will soon have just
four from which to choose, and I believe that the panel will make an informed judgment
as to the final four. It remains then simply for the people to speak, and having spoken—
by definition infallibly —we can move on to the truly important constitutional issues
confronting the Realm of New Zealand that continue to cry out for attention.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : There should be, I think, at least three categories
of consideration for a flag change. The first is that there needs to be an appropriate
context for it. Such a context could be, for example, a proposal for a republic, or at least
a debate on a wide range of real constitutional questions such as Māori seats, a written
constitution, the size of Parliament, the size and number of electorates, the length of the
parliamentary term, Māori electoral options and participation, and the role of the Treaty
of Waitangi. But there is no such context for this bill. That context is missing altogether.
Therefore, there is little or nothing to inform the reason for the change  of a flag on this
occasion, which might, in turn, have informed the kind of flag that could be needed if,
indeed, there was to be any change at all. Of course, New Zealand First denies that.
Secondly, the process for this kind of change needs to be drive n from the bottom-up,
not the top- down. This proposal is out of the blue from John Key —just his latest big
idea, and, as usual, his bad idea. It risks, as it has done already in this case, undue
politicisation and, therefore, divisiveness when we really ne ed efforts to encourage
unity in this country. But Mr Key is not interested in that. No doubt the PM has his own
agenda. We are all expected to dance to his tune. But the consultation process has
shown no public pressure for change. The roadshow that toure d the country has been
extremely poorly supported, with a very modest response online as well. The third
category is that the process needs to be fair, understandable, and uncomplicated, but this
process is none of those things. The process is not fair, because the first flag referendum
effectively disenfranchises people who want the current 1902 flag. But they cannot
express those feelings in the first referendum; therefore, the turnout is bound to be
pretty low. I predict it will be lower than 25 percent. And there will also be many spoilt
votes because the process is essentially undemocratic for the reason I just gave.
Also, the process is not understandable. Some may well think that the first
referendum is the only referendum on the flag and that they must choose a new flag
because the current one, of course, is not there at all. They will think that the current one
is to be dumped, whatever they want. This lack of understandability is caused by the
unnecessary complexity of the two- referendum system, one of which is totally back to
front. One referendum would have been enough, either by asking first whether a flag
change is wanted at all —which a normal, common- sense person would have done, but
not this Government —or at least adding the current flag to the first referendum as one
of the choices, thereby making the second referendum completely redundant.
It is now perfectly clear that the vast majority of New Zealanders are asking why we
would even consider a new flag, especially now, in a year when we are remembering
those who fought under the current flag at Gallipoli 100 years ago. One hundred years
ago this month was t he battle of Chunuk Bair. It is the efforts of brave Kiwis at that
battle that have defined New Zealand as a truly independent nation. I want to read some
excerpts from a recent newspaper article about that. The first says this: “The
commander of the Wellington battalion Colonel William Malone never received the
acknowledgment he was owed for his role. He cared deeply for his men, and when his
British commanders ordered him to attack Chunuk Bair in daylight he defied them,
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5823
saying: ‘We are not taking orders from you people. My men are not going to commit
suicide.’ ” Further on, in another article, it is stated: “Chunuk Bair is also seen as [key
to] … the development of a distinct New Zealand identity, not least because of the
perception that Kiwis and Austral ians were treated as cannon fodder by bumbling
British officers.” Later in the same articles it says: “And when it comes to Gallipoli
there’s the added significance that this was the first time New Zealanders had been
deployed … [as] distinct from Britain … ‘It was foundational in the development of our
national identity.’ ”
This very month is the moment that John Key, the ever -silent Prime Minister on this
issue and in this debate, and his worn- out National Government have chosen to push a
new flag on New  Zealanders. This is the moment he chooses to do that. How grossly
insensitive to the men who died at Chunuk Bair. How deeply disrespectful to the flag
they fought under. How totally badly timed in terms of context to be parading the
incredibly awful long list of new flag designs we have seen recently —those gaudy,
ugly, dull designs, most of which look more like logos for a pound of butter than they
do a flag of the stature of New Zealand. One of them —the one with a white fern on a
black flag, which I under stand the Prime Minister favours —looks more like the Jolly
Roger from a pirate ship. It is totally, totally inappropriate and out of touch with our
rich Māori, Pacific, and British heritage.
The current flag is not out of date, as those members opposite w ould have us believe.
It is as appropriate today as it was in 1902, when officially adopted. It represents,
through the Union Jack in the corner, the British heritage of New Zealand—the
Scottish, the Irish, and the English heritage —the English language, le gal system, and
culture, and the Westminster system of Government. All of those things are our heritage
and are just as much the Kiwi heritage as they are the British heritage, and that is why
that flag should stay in the corner of the New Zealand flag. But the flag also represents
our Pacific and Māori heritage through the Southern Cross, which tells of the amazing
feats of navigation and resilience by ancient Māori people finding their way across the
vast Pacific Ocean and settling Aotearoa, and who are n ow the tāngata whenua of the
land.
There is, in New Zealand First’s view, only one appropriate response to the first flag
referendum for anyone who respects the current flag and who wants to keep the current
flag. Either those people, and they are going t o be the majority, should not vote at all —
they should stay away. Or, alternatively, they may draw a vote, but not choose any of
the four alternatives shown and return a blank vote. That would be proper. Or, if they
wish, they could write “I want the current flag.” across the ballot paper, choose none of
the alternatives, and put that in the ballot box. That would be appropriate as well. Given
the gerrymandered and inappropriate nature of this non- referendum, this failed and
flawed process, New Zealand First calls on Kiwis to do any one of those things to show
their disgust, not just at the timing and the process for this referendum but the
gerrymandered nature of it. The fact is that they want to keep the current flag, just as
New Zealand First wants to.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and take a call in this third
reading of the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill. The third reading is a great
opportunity to reflect on some of the arguments that have been made in the first reading,
the second reading, the Committee of the whole House, and the Justice and Electoral
Committee, and on what has already been said at the third reading. For a start, I have
got to pick up on the last comment that Mr  O’Rourke made in the previous speech,
when he was inciting, I guess, civil disobedience in some way, shape, or form by
encouraging people to spoil voting papers or not to vote at all. I hope that he does
5824 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
remember to tell them to make sure they vote in the  second referendum if they are not
going to vote in the first one.
There have been some really interesting arguments put forward as to why people
should vote this down, and I want to reflect on some of them. The first one, which has
been brought up a lot, has been the order of the questions, with people suggesting that
we should have a yes/no vote first. This was put forward in the Committee of the whole
House by a number of members, but possibly most eloquently by Kris Faafoi the other
day, who likened choosing a new flag to having a new car. His argument was that if you
are going to get another car, you should decide whether or not you want another car
before deciding what kind you want. I was reflecting on this, and I was thinking of my
wife’s Suzuki Swi ft. If somebody said to her “Do you want another car?”, she might
say: “Well, yes. But it would depend on what it is.” Because if somebody was offering
her a brand new Lamborghini, the answer might be yes; if someone was offering her a
1972 Ford Cortina, t he answer might be no. So I think it is really important that we do
get these questions in the right order, and this is the right order to have them in. It is the
most logical.
By having the referendum split across two referendums and by putting them in this
order, it is allowing absolutely everybody to participate. If you do not want a change to
the New Zealand flag, you can still choose a potential alternative in the first
referendum—or you can choose not to vote if that is what you want to do. Then the
second referendum will decide which of those flags you want. If you definitely want
change, you get to participate. If you definitely do not want change, you get to
participate. But if you ask the yes/no question first, all of those people who are saying
that it depends on what the options are will be excluded from the debate. Mr O’Rourke
says that he wants everyone to participate. Everyone will get to participate, and if they
choose to participate in only the second referendum that is OK —that is their business—
because the first referendum is subservient to the second referendum.
The other thing that has been said, and Mr O’Rourke mentioned it a number of times
in the Committee of the whole House, is how gormless the alternatives are. He used the
words “gaudy ” and “ugly” today, and he said that the alternatives were all in this
category. I find this a little bit disturbing because one of the arguments that has been put
forward is that the current flag is the flag that New Zealand soldiers died and fought
under. Actually, a whole heap of those alternative designs that have been put forward
have got the silver fern on them. I can tell Mr O’Rourke that, actually, if you want to
have a sense of right dealings with people who have died for New Zealand—if you have
a look at every New Zealand war grave, you will see that there is a silver fern on it —
referring to the silver fern as “gormless”, “gaudy”, or “ugly” is, I think, a whole lot
more disrespectful than whatever else has been talked about in this argument, as we
have gone through it.
The other thing that has been really interesting is to observe the Labour Party’s
approach to this debate. At least, it was quite good in the Committee of the whole
House the other day. Mr Lees -Galloway finally —because not many Labour members
have been willing to do it —admitted that it was the Labour Party policy to change the
flag going into the last election. We did invite him to read out what the policy said but
he declined, so I will do so for the House right now. It says this: “L abour will: review
the design of the New Zealand flag involving flag design experts and with full public
consultation and involvement.” So that is OK. The Labour Party was talking about that,
and that is all right. But the argument that he put forward, and it has been put forward
again by Mr Robertson today, saying to defer it for 5 years —Mr Mallard was
suggesting that perhaps we defer it further —is kind of interesting, because if you read
the next line in the Labour Party policy, it says: “We believe that the time has come for
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5825
a change …”. It does not say: “We believe that in 5 years’ time, the time might come.”

items.speaker: The Labour Party policy says
items.text: “We believe that the time has come for a change …”. I
think that is kind of fascinating.
The other thing that Labour members keep saying too is that this is a vanity project—
a vanity project of the Prime Minister. They say: “Oh, it’s vanity. Oh, it’s all down to
the vanity of the Prime Minister as to why we are doing this now.” As I said the other
day, when somebody put this in the Labour Party policy, whose vanity was it then?
Because that is what those members are telling us: it is all about vanity —it is all about
vanity. It was in the Labour Party policy, and so whose vanity was it then? The other
thing that has been really interesting is that during the 2014 election campaign Labour’s
then leader—I keep losing track —Mr David Cunliffe kept accusing the National Party
of stealing Labour Party policies. We have a bill before us right now that is absolutely,
in black and white—or red and white if you print it in colour —Labour Party policy, and
Labour wants to vote against it. I do not understand it. There is no logic, but that is the
Labour Party for you.
What we have heard from Mr O’Rourke already, and what we have heard f rom the
Labour Party again today, is that the Prime Minister has got it wrong. He said that this
will be the end of the Prime Minister —that he is forcing something on the people that
they do not want. Well, I would say that nominally what those members are  saying is:
“We don’t like the Prime Minister and want to see him fall over.” If you are so
convinced that this is a bad idea and if you want to get rid of the National Party and you
want to get rid of the Prime Minister, then I dare you to vote for this bill, because what
you are saying is completely illogical. So get behind it and vote for it if you are so
convinced this is a bad idea and that it will be the undoing of the National Party.
What is this bill about? We have had three flags before. They have all been chosen
by the Government of the day or by others, but for the first time in New Zealand’s
history, New Zealanders will get to choose what their national emblem is —what the
New Zealand flag is. They will get to choose. They may well choose the 1902 flag—the
flag that we have now —and that will be their democratic right, but this party, the
National Party of New Zealand, is absolutely keen to ensure that New Zealanders have
their say and that they get to decide what is important to them. I am looking forward to
passing this bill so that we can take this out of the political domain of this House and
put it into the hands of the people of New Zealand, where it belongs.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. I call
Dr Russel Norman.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I rise on behalf of the Green Party to speak on the
New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill. This bill, of course, is a classic form over
substance bill. The form, of course, is what the actual pattern is on the flag —the flag
that flies out in front of Parliament, the flag that is on all of the New Zealand First
benches in here today, the flag that is here, there, and everywhere.
But, you know, at the end of the day a flag is a pattern. So, really, it is about saying
that some people want to change the pattern. But the reason why the pattern of a flag
matters is that it actually refers to a deeper substance, and the deeper substance that it
refers to is about the constitutional arrangements of the country. That is the thing that
really matters.
Part of the reason why, I guess, New Zealand First is pretty agitated about it is that it
sees the Union Jack in th e corner of the flag as representing the monarchy and the links
to the monarchy—and fair enough. You know, I can understand that, but if you believe
in independence and democracy and you want to cut the links to the monarchy, to
actually have a proper repu blican democracy involving the Treaty of Waitangi, then, of
course, you do not particularly want the Union Jack on the flag.
5826 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
What the Government is proposing to do is to change the pattern without changing
any of the substance. So it is having this big kind of hoopla and saying “Oh, we’re
doing something really substantive. We’re doing something very important. We’re
doing something big. This is big; this is visionary. We’re changing the flag.”, as if
something underneath were changing. But, of course, nothing whatsoever is changing
underneath. The Prime Minister awarded Prince Philip an Order of New Zealand, for
goodness’ sake, just like Tony Abbott did. Basically, it has been years since we have
had such a fawning Prime Minister over the British monarchy. I mean, I have never
seen anything like it. So in terms of the substance underneath it, nothing changes.
If you wanted a referendum that actually had real substance, the asset sales
referendum was a referendum about real substance: should we privatise thes e assets?
People voted not to privatise the assets; the Government completely ignored them, of
course. What it really wants is a show, and so we are going to have the flag debate
show, which is really what the Government wants, rather than discussing the t rue
substance.
At this very moment we are having a debate about the Trans -Pacific Partnership,
which changes the constitutional arrangements of New Zealand in a very fundamental
way, through the investor -State dispute settlement clauses. As the former Dire ctor-
General of the World Trade Organization said, they are writing a new constitution for a
new world order. So that fundamentally changes the New Zealand constitution, by
setting up a judicial system outside of New Zealand. At the same time as we are hav ing
this show called the flag debate, all about what the pattern on this flag should be, over
here the Government is actually, fundamentally, really altering the constitution to take
away the democratic right of decision making over Government policy. That , of course,
is the reality of what is going on. So the show goes on over here: a show about the flag
and what should be printed on the flag.
Over here, the reality goes on: power is being taken away from ordinary New
Zealanders and assets are being sold. Those are the real issues. In terms of the
relationship with the British Crown and the ridiculous idea that the head of State should
be determined by birth —ha, ha! What a ridiculous idea. Let us have the head of State
determined by birth—you know, what if someone came up with that? “Oh, we’re going
to let them be chosen by birth.” What a great way to choose the head of State! So
instead of having a debate about something real and substantive —whether the head of
State should be chosen by the Parliament or by  the people through an election,
something like that; an actual, substantive thing —we are going to have the flag show.
We are going to have the flag show, and the Prime Minister will say that this is his
thing. This is his great vision of independence for the country.
At the same time he is actually selling out our independence and our real democracy
and the things that really matter: the ability to determine what kinds of regulation we
have about the environment and about health care. They are stripping aw ay, through the
Trans-Pacific Partnership and other kinds of deals like that, the right of people to
actually determine the issues that really matter to people —about environmental
protection; well, you name it.
So one of the real issues for the Greens in t his is that we are having this debate
around this pattern, which is all about optics and the Prime Minister’s vision, so that it
looks like he has a long -term vision for this country, while at the same time the real
issues that really matter —another 45,000 children living in poverty, as we discovered
today—are being swept under the carpet and, actually, swept under the carpet behind
the light show that is the Prime Minister’s flag show.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Marama Fox—5 minutes.
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5827

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: I rise to take a call on this very
important discussion. I think it is an important discussion becaus e I absolutely agree
with a lot of the objections about why we are doing this. But, actually, I absolutely
agree that I would like to see a change in the flag, because I would like to see something
that does symbolise our duality of nationhood. Should we be spending this amount of
money on doing it? I would like to think not. Should we have put a constitutional
change in first, before we put a flag change in? I absolutely agree with that. I would
love to see us talk about the constitution in very real ways,  which is why the Māori
Party wanted to have the constitutional review —and that is what has happened—based
on the Treaty of Waitangi. A constitution that sees us into our young adulthood as a
nation, that brings us forward into our future, with a symbol of  our new nationhood, our
independence, our forward- thinking nation built on a constitution of partnership with
the Treaty at its base—I think that would be amazing.
But we do not have that opportunity. Right now we have this big debate about how
much it costs, about whether we are disrespecting our fallen soldiers, about all of those
things, and really we are missing the opportunity to talk about this symbol that
encapsulates who we are as a nation. Should it have been round the other way? I
absolutely agre e. It should have been. But I do not worry about what other people’s
agendas are. I want to know what our people think. If we get caught up in talking about
everything else, we will miss the opportunity to pick a symbol, to choose something that
truly represents us.
I have listened to Mr O’Rourke’s comments about our fallen warriors and the flag
and what it represents. I actually disagree. I do not think that our soldiers fought for a
flag. They fought under a flag, yes they did, but they fought for each other, and they
fought for their families, and they fought for the right to be free and to express our
freedoms. Our warriors, our Māori Battalion, our Hokowhitu- a-Tū, went to that same
war, those same battles, and gave their lives under a flag that actuall y, at the time, did
not recognise their right to be free people. Under that flag they came home and were not
treated in the same way. They were not given land. They were not given an allowance.
They were disrespected under that flag. When they went to war they were not even
given a weapon. So, actually, I say: they fought for what? For the price of citizenship,
under a flag that did not recognise their greatness. We do now—we do now.
So let us move forward. Let us move forward as a nation and take the opportunity to
have the discussion, because if we get caught up in the discussion that is only about the
money and all of those things, then we will miss the opportunity.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Who’s disrespecting them now?

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: I do not think it is disrespecting them. You can still fly the Union
Jack, this flag that is proudly represented on the benches over here. You can still fly that
flag if you want to, but I think it is time to move us forward into a new generation t hat
represents the duality of our nationhood, where I can proudly see myself as a Māori
citizen of this country. My ancestors fought for the right just to speak their own
language in this country. My ancestors fought for the right to live on their own land, to
practise their own culture, and I want to see a flag that represents their struggle. I do not
see that in this flag right now. I would like to take the opportunity for our people to
come together to have that discussion and really think about what the  symbol is that
encapsulates our desire as a nation to stand together and be united, recognising our
duality of nationhood, our united history, our Māori history, and our non- Māori
history—whatever culture that is —and have it reflected in a flag as a symbo l of unity
for our country.
5828 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
I quite like the red, black, and white flag with the fern, but I would not mind seeing
the Matariki stars on it. We talk about navigation. There are a few stars that are missing.
That is why we are going to support this referendum, and I proudly do so. Kia ora.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: There are at least two parties in th is Parliament that
are in favour of a referendum on changing the New Zealand flag. There is the
Government party—the National Party; we are in favour of a referendum on changing
the flag —and the Labour Party. Labour members are in favour of a referendum on
changing the flag. They just do not have the guts to turn up in this House—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I know what the member  is going
to bring up. I would ask the member to withdraw that comment. This is a seemly debate,
and comments like that do not add any value. Just withdraw the comment and then carry
on.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: I withdraw. They do not have the intestinal fortitude—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That has been ruled out
many times. This is now repeated offending. [Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am on my feet. I will ask the
member to withdraw that comment. We will not have any more of those sorts of
comments.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: I withdraw. It is a real shame that the Labour Party is voting
against this bill. It is the official policy of the Labour Party to have a flag referendum, to
have a referendum on changing the flag. The leader of the Labour Party wants to change
the flag, or at least he wants to consider changing the flag, and he wants to do it in a
deliberative and consultative fashion. We know that, because he told the National
Business Review  and he told a commenter in the “Ask Me Anything” section in the
National Business Review . We know that most Labour Party MPs, I believe, are in
favour of a flag referendum. Probably Labour Party members, ordinary grassroots
members of the Labour Party —as few as they are—are in favour of a referendum on
changing the flag. So it is a real shame that this is not a bipartisan bill.
This bill is fundamentally about a conversation about who we are as people. It is a
conversation and it is a discussion about what New Zealand is in the 21 st century.
Symbols do matter. The flag  does matter. Do we want the Union Jack on the flag? In
21st century New Zealand, with our multiplicity of ethnicities and peoples who exist, for
the most part, harmoniously in this country, do we really want the symbol or the
message on our flag to be that we are a vassal of mother Britain, of the mother country?
Do we really want that in the 21 st century, with New Zealand today, with all of its
complexity, with all of its diversity, and, quite frankly, without the links back to the
United Kingdom? So symbols do matter. That is what this bill is about.
Also, this bill is about a democratic process to choose the design of a potential or
putative new New Zealand flag. The Government could have legislated for a new New
Zealand flag. We could have done that. We  could have put it in the National Party
manifesto, before the last election, that we would legislate for a new New Zealand flag.
Other countries have done that. When Canada changed its flag, that is essentially what
they did. We could have done that. But no, the Government chose not to do that. What
the Government chose to do was involve the people. I believe that is the right thing to
do. I believe the right thing to do is to ask the people what sort of flag they want,
because, as I mentioned, this is abo ut a conversation with the New Zealand people as to
what New Zealand represents, what New Zealand is in the 21 st century. So it is right
that we ask the people.
The great thing about the process so far is that New Zealanders want that
conversation to happe n—they do. If you look at the New Zealand Herald polls and at
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5829
the designs that have been submitted, and you look at the number of people who are
getting involved online and talking about it at the water coolers, every single day that
goes by more and more people are having those conversations. They are getting a coffee
and they are talking about it. I hear it when I go into cafes. I hear people grabbing a
drink and talking about it. I hear it in pubs and clubs. I hear people talking about what
the change sh ould be. People are talking about whether they want the blue and red
design with the silver fern or whether it would be better to have a blue and black design.
Is it appropriate to have a Southern Cross on it or not? Should we go for something
completely different? The 40 flags that have come down on to the long list are really
provoking debate out there. So this is about a democratic process to choose the design.
We are not just legislating for a change of flag; we are legislating for a process.
If, after the second referendum, New Zealanders do not want a change of flag, well,
that would be the people’s say; that would be the people’s verdict. But I reckon people
are actually getting pretty excited about this process and I reckon we are going to see
good participation in both referenda, and I think that is good.
I want to run through some of the arguments that have been raised by the Labour
Party members and other people about why this bill should fail. Firstly, they say this is
not the right time. Well, I mean, really? Is any time ever the right time? People have
been trying to change the flag since the 1970s. This was first raised in the 1970s. You
can make that argument about any time. The Labour Party says: “Oh, well, let’s do it in
5 years.” Why 5 years? That is totally arbitrary. Why not 10? Why not 7? Why not in 2
years? It is just bizarre.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: It’s politicking.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: It is just bizarre, and it is just politicking, as my colleague points
out, and it is a real shame. It would have been nice for this to be bipartisan. I do not
accept the argument that now is not the right time.
Then we have this absurd argument that nobody wants a change of flag. Why? Oh,
because we looked at the opinion polls. We ll, actually, we are going to have a giant
opinion poll about it; it is called the referendum on changing the flag. Everyone will get
to have a say, and it will not be a cursory show of public opinion before we have had
the proper debate, before people have managed to see the options, before people have
managed to make up their own mind. We are going to have a giant opinion poll; it is
called a referendum, and it is going to be next year.
So this absurd argument that we can just take a slice of public opini on from the New
Zealand Herald online poll at a particular point or something, and say that therefore we
should not go through with a referendum is a silly argument. On the same basis, we
would have taken a slice of public opinion on 19 September before the last election and
gone “Oh, well, National’s on 54 percent; the Labour Party’s on 18 percent.” —or
something like that—“and we won’t bother with the election.” No, we do not govern
like that in this country. We put it to the people.
Thirdly, we had this a rgument that there are other priorities. There is this ridiculous
argument that as a Government you can do only one thing at one time in this country;
you cannot do two things at once. There are other priorities. The nadir of this argument
was Andrew Littl e’s ridiculous claim this week. This is the potential future Prime
Minister of this country.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: Unlikely.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: Very unlikely, my colleague Michael Woodhouse points out. His
claim is this r idiculous comment that he is not even going to bother to vote in the first
referendum. He is not even going to bother. The potential future Prime Minister of this
country, whose own party has a policy of having a referendum on the flag, is not even
going to bother to vote. Well, how ridiculous! The reality of Government is, amazingly,
5830 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
in the grown-up world on the side of the Government, not “Planet Labour”, that you can
do two things at once. We can improve the economy, we can improve social housing,
we can focus on the least well -off in society, and we can do that contemporaneously by
having a referendum on a flag. We are grown-ups on this side of the House, not children
in the sandpit like members opposite.
Fourthly, we have the silly argument that this di srespects veterans, and this is allied
to the argument that was raised by, I think, the member for New Zealand First that
people fight for the flag. Well, actually, I put it respectfully that the people who have
fought for this country do not fight for a piece of cloth; they fought, and they do fight,
for the values that underlie the flag. I have been to Gallipoli and I have seen the
memorials and I have seen the graves, and it is not the New Zealand flag that exists now
that is on those memorials—it is not—it is the silver fern. So I do not buy the argument
that this disrespects veterans and it disrespects the sacrifice that they have made. I do
not.
Then we hear that this is a waste of money. This is also a silly argument. In the grand
scheme of Government spending, $26 million is not a large sum of money. We did not
hear the Labour Party members complaining about a waste of public money when we
had a referendum on asset sales. They did not make that argument at the time, so I also
do not buy the argument that this is a waste of money.
Then, finally, we had the argument that we need an up or down, yes or no, vote in the
first referendum. This was an argument that was put by Trevor Mallard in his petition
and by Labour members of the Justice and Electoral Committee. The official advice that
we received as a select committee was that this would not be a good idea—that we
should not have a yes or no vote in the first referendum. Why? Because, quite rightly,
people want to know what they are voting for before the y vote for whether or not they
want to change the flag. That is a legitimate point of view. People have a right to know
in a binary sense what the options are, and that is why Government members do not
accept that.
This is an important bill about an important part of New Zealand’s future. It is a
shame that the Labour Party is voting against this bill, not because it does not agree with
it, not because members do not potentially want a change of flag, but because they are
based only on spite and jealousy.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Jenny
Salesa—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: I rise to take this call on this very
costly and wasteful bill, the New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill. The New Zealand
flag is significant to many of us. It is an emotional point of connection for all New
Zealanders, and it can be a rallying point, a unifying icon, and a brand that is of benefit
to Aotearoa New Zealand.
However, there are an increasing number of New Zealanders who have joined the
Labour Party in opposing this bill and the expensive flag referendums process that we
are just undergoing . Many do not support the process or the spending of millions of
dollars on the flag referendums. I would also like to point out that the decision of what
four designs will actually be put through on the referendum will not necessarily be from
the consultation process. It is a decision that Cabinet will actually make.
People know what is actually important to them. In the last few weeks the Labour
Party MPs called together a lot of people in my electorate, in Ōtara in Manukau East,
for a housing meeting. Over 120 people came to that meeting, on a cold, freezing, rainy
Saturday afternoon in the middle of winter. Contrast that to one of the other meetings,
which was a flag referendum meeting, held in the same electorate at Ōtāhuhu, where
only 34 people attended. Lest it be said that Manukau East is an anomaly here, I would
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5831
like to point out that at the very first flag referendum meeting held in Takapuna, only 13
people could be bothered to attend that meeting. There has been a total of only about
700 people across New Zealand who have actually turned out to public meetings on the
flag project, and this is at a cost, on average, of about $550 per person. However, when
you take into account the exorbitant fees of the panel members and venue hire, this
amount rises to a shocking $2,300 per person.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: It is $2,300 when you include the price of advertising.
The people of South Auckland and elsewhere have shown this Government what is
actually important to them, by attending the forums on issues that matter to them and
their families. They attended the meeting on housing in South Auckland because they
are desperate to have maintenance issues on their houses fixed —their houses that are
leaky, damp, and mouldy —and they also attended because the rent is becoming way,
way too expensive in our electorate. Housing is what matters to our families, not this
wasteful vanity project on a flag referendum. What is the Government’s solution to the
housing crisis? That is right: it is proposing to sell thousands of our State houses. I can
assure you that it did not cost $2,300 per person to run our South Auckland meeting on
housing; in fact, it cost the Government nothing at all because the hall was free —it was
a church hall —and the organisers of the meeting brought the refreshments for the
meeting.
The engagement with the public on the flag has been very poor: 747 Kiwis wanted to
be heard at the Justice and Electoral Committee, but their request to be heard was
refused; 43,000 people signed a petition asking for a yes/no vote on the flag, and they
were also ignored.
Already we have spent $8.4 million on this process. We should not be contemplating
spending an additional $17.3 million to distract Kiwis from the S erco scandals, the
appalling mis -administration of charter schools, and the continuing job losses in
important industries, to name but a few.
I also want to address what the members Jono Naylor and Chris Bishop on the
opposite side of the House said, who a ctually stated what Labour’s policy on the flag
referendum is. May I just say that we are focused on actually addressing issues that
matter for our people. The questions that I ask are: can we afford this expensive $26
million on a flag at this time? Has this current Government produced the Budget surplus
that it has promised? Well, the answer is no, not yet.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Nanaia Mahuta —5
minutes.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: If this was a vote based
purely on choosing a symbol, I think it would be quite easy, but it is not. Symbols do
matter. Flags of a country and nation matt er. What Labour is saying is that what sits
behind the flag —the constitutional arrangements —is so important. Yet this particular
bill has reduced the debate down to process, not principles and priorities.
My colleagues have been absolutely right in pointing out the inefficiencies of this
particular process. The Government is treating Kiwis with contempt about significant
questions affecting them. It is not simply good enough to say “Let’s choose a flag.”, and
then the issue of the national anthem will come up, and then: “Let’s discuss that, and
then maybe the Governor -General.” That is constitutional creep; it is not constitutional
reform with a purpose that takes New Zealand confidently into the future. The Prime
Minister is treating Kiwis with contempt, be cause those significant issues are not being
put in front of this very important issue, which is the question of what symbol should
best represent us as a nation.
5832 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
I heard the impassioned contribution made by the Māori Party. In part, there are lots
of members in this House who would agree with that sentiment. However, I think that
choosing a symbol before the very legitimate debate about what our constitutional
arrangements and the place of the Treaty should be is in advance of a very important
type of cons ideration. I predict that the New Zealand flag will be changed, but I also
predict that should this bill go ahead in the way that the Government is promoting, very
soon we will see, in pockets of New Zealand, a number of communities that affiliate
with a p articular flag flying their own flag. Is that the symbol for the country? I think
not. Is that the type of New Zealand we want to see—where people will have an affinity
with different types of flag and fly them because they cannot have an attachment to the
outcome of this referendum? I think that is the worst outcome of all.
What I am really fearful of is that because of the way that this particular referendum
is constructed, it will be a flag for the 1 percent —$25.7 million spent on a process to
deliver a flag for 1 percent is not good enough.
Out in simple communities where people want to make a living they are saying: a
flag or feed children; a flag or warm homes; a flag or provide houses in our community
for people who need them. That is the type of cons ideration that people are weighing up
when they are listening to this particular debate—$25.7 million on this exercise.
Asking a question in advance of some significant, weighty issues around what the
constitution of this country represents and what the sy mbol of identity represents is, I
think, a farce in itself. People who know me know that I have no particular affinity with
the New Zealand flag, but I will defend it for what it represents for this country. The
history of my own particular area is that we  have a particular flag for our iwi, but we
will defend the New Zealand flag because we understand that it represents an evolving
sense of identity that we can hold on to, that holds the Crown accountable for its
commitment to tangata whenua, to Māori.
The member Alfred Ngaro raised the issue of Mat Rata. Mat said a number of things
in his history. When he made that particular comment it was just before the fisheries
settlement. The fisheries settlement was the first pan -Māori settlement where the
Government attempted to do something in, I believe, a quite progressive way.
Underpinning his comments, I believe, was his understanding that the Treaty had a
place in the future of New Zealand. He established the Waitangi Tribunal. He led the
challenge for this pa n-Māori settlement, which could transform the nation. Just on
Wednesday we had numerous debates about how Treaty of Waitangi settlements have
transformed the national identity of our nation.
Well, the world has moved on and New Zealand has moved on. Our national identity
is progressing; however, underpinning the choice of a flag must be the constitutional
arrangements of this country. That is why I stand in support of my colleagues in the
Labour Party who are opposing this based on process but, more funda mentally, based
on principle. Any symbol of this country must give all Kiwis confidence that it is
something that we can all hold on to. This one does not.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I feel very proud of what we are
on the cusp of doing tonight, and that is giving the people of New Zealand an
opportunity to do exactly what three out of four people voted to be able to do less than
12 months ago.
I always listen to the Hon Nanaia Mahuta with respect, and she knows I hold her in
high regard. I have listened carefully to her arguments and I acknowledge some of them,
but I ask her to look around her colleagues and to think carefully about some of the
arguments that they have advance d. She must be ashamed of some of the contributions
that Labour members have made to this debate, and of the fact that a party would put
aside principle to go for short -term, populist interests because they seem, at the
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5833
moment, to resonate with the public because there is a certain mood out there. She
needs to reflect again on the fact that the Labour Party went to the 2014 election, less
than 12 months ago, saying that it had a policy that aims to “enhance knowledge,
appreciation and pride in New Zealand’s  identity, history, biculturalism,
multiculturalism and other diversity, community resilience, distinctiveness … through a
review of the design of the New Zealand flag involving flag design experts and with full
public consultation and involvement.” —in other words, exactly what we have just had
and what we are continuing to do.
I want to commend all 40 of those designs that have been short -listed. Some of them,
of course, are by the same designer, but there are a large number of designers whose
work is repr esented there. They reflect a variety of symbols that give us choice, and I
have to say I would be very proud for a large number of those to be the New Zealand
flag, but I am going to put on record that, along with many people, I personally opt for
the Kyle Lockwood red and blue fern with a Southern cross flag, and I will explain why
in a moment.
I am absolutely appalled at the claptrap we have had to listen to, particularly from the
Labour Party, but also from its friends in the Greens. There is absolutely  no doubt that
the vast majority of members of both of those parties want change in this area. They
must be astonished that their representatives in this House have come here and are
suddenly arguing for no change on an issue that they have all talked about for a very
long time, in many cases for many generations.
When I spoke in the second reading of this debate I explained why it is quite a
personal issue for me. We have heard a lot about what our military men and women
may feel on this issue. I made the point that I am the great grandson, the grandson, the
son, and the nephew of men who fought in the New Zealand Army in the great conflicts
of the late 19 th and the 20 th centuries: the Boer War, the First World War, and the
Second World War. My uncle Ken wa s killed in action right at the end of the Second
World War, and he is buried in southern Italy. Along with all of those who could tell a
similar story of being the descendants of people who fought for our country, they would
all acknowledge that the thing those men, and in some cases women, have in common is
that they are buried with a symbol that is not the New Zealand flag—
Su’a William Sio: Smile, Tim. Smile.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: It is not the New Zealand flag, Mr Sio; it is the silver fern.
Su’a William Sio: Smile.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I will smile if you would like me to, because I am proud of what
we are doing. I would say to Mr Sio that rather than treating this issue like a village
idiot, he too should turn to his colleagues and say: “This is serious, and we are letting
down the people who voted for us.” Those who voted Labour at the last election voted
for what we are doing here today, and I cannot believe that Labour is turning its back on
its own policy less than a year later and trying to pretend that somehow it is doing this
on a point of principle.
I agreed with Marama Fox when she said earlier that the New Zealand men and
women who have fought for this country fought for freedom, they fought for values,
and they fought to maintain the way of life that we hold dear. Some may ha ve had a
sense of pride in a flag, but they did not fight for that flag; they fought for our country
and for those who are allied to us and who share those values and who wanted to
supress tyranny and fight back against tyranny. I say to them “Thank you for that
service.”, and that is why I believe that at this time —far from Mr Mallard’s argument
that it is disrespectful to be having this debate now —there is no better time for us to
honour the legacy of those men and women than as we mark the centenary of G allipoli
and the 100-year period since World War I of 1914 to 1918.
5834 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015
As we look at those who through the ages in New Zealand’s relatively short history
have fought for us, I believe that the symbol that they would most want to have on our
flag is the symbol that is on their graves: the silver fern. It is as simple as that. That is
why although I do believe in change in this issue, I particularly want the fern on our
flag. I am proud of my British heritage, and most of us in this House —certainly not all,
but most of us—have some British heritage. The Union Jack is a fantastic flag. If I were
British I would wear it, I would fly it, and I would proudly display it at all opportunities.
But we are not British. We are 12,500 miles away, and it is a very long time since we
were a British colony. The time, therefore, in my view, is right to take that colonial
emblem off our flag and to reassert our independence as a modern and progressive
nation.
I am absolutely sick of having the confusion with the Australian flag c onstantly
thrown at us. When people are overseas and asked to identify the New Zealand flag,
hardly anyone can. Fifty years ago the Canadians had the same argument because they
had a similar flag —it was just predominantly red instead of the blue that we ha ve got.
They had the same issue, they changed to a symbol that they all identified with, the
maple leaf, and which one of them would go back to that old flag now? Not one of
them, because they all now feel incredibly proud of that emblem that they wear and they
fly and they display on their backpacks that says, unashamedly: “We are Canadian.
Well, I want something that says: “We’re New Zealanders and let’s be recognised as
New Zealanders right around the world.” The silver fern will do that, but I also want  to
retain the stars of the Southern Cross. That is why I like that Kyle Lockwood design,
because of the Southern Cross with the stars that guided our Māori ancestors to this
land. To my mind that is a wonderful way of honouring that legacy of the tangata
whenua of this land while also putting something on the flag that we all embrace as
New Zealanders of a modern era.
As I said, I am absolutely appalled by the duplicity and the populist hypocrisy of the
2015 version of the Labour Party, which cannot even honour its own 2014 election
policy. What an abuse of trust. For the leader of the Labour Party this year to say that he
will not even vote in an election, when last year he went on record and said that this is
absolutely the right thing, that this is what we should be doing, and that this is the way
to go about it, is absolutely abominable.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. If New Zealanders do not vote to change the
flag this time, most of us will not see the opportunity come again in our lifetime —
maybe some of the younger members will, but most of us will not—and here we are
being told that the cost is an issue. Well, it is the first time that New Zealanders have
been given a chance— all of them—to say: “This is the flag I want.” What price
democracy? It is an important decision to be made, and I would suggest to you that it is
money that is worth spending and it is worth doing the process correctly.
I cannot believe that there are some who would argue that because there are other
things we could spe nd the money on— and of course there always will be—we should
not do it. Well, that argument will apply next year and the year after, and in 5 years’
time. That will never change. At some point we have to spend the money, and I believe
spending the money on  having a truly democratic decision on this particular issue is
really important.
I will go back to the other issue that Mr Mallard raised earlier about going to tell the
RSA what I think. I will accept an invitation from any RSA around the country to go
and have this discussion, because I find when I talk to returned servicemen and women
that they do understand the argument when it is put. I repeat that I believe that we are
honouring them, their service, and particularly those of their comrades who paid t he
ultimate sacrifice, by having the symbol that is on the tombstones across Western
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5835
Europe put on to their graves. I am, as I said at the outset of this speech, incredibly
proud of the opportunity that we are delivering to the country. I am incredibly proud as
a National MP that we are honouring the commitment that we took to the country last
year and that we are standing by the policy that we campaigned on, and I remind
everybody listening that nearly three in every four people who voted in last year’s
election voted for this. So let us get on and do what they voted for.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the New Zealand Flag Referendums
Bill be now read a third time.
Ayes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 56
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 12; New Zealand First 12.
Bill read a third time.

13 Aug 2015 Business Statement 5783 
 
THURSDAY, 13 AUGUST 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : When the House resumes on 
Tuesday, 18 August the Government will look to make progress on the Health and 
Safety Reform Bill and the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill. 
MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS 
Solid Energy—Voluntary Administration 
Hon TODD McCLAY (Minister for State Owned Enterprises) : I wish to make a 
ministerial statement under Standing Order 356 in relation to Solid Energy going into 
voluntary administration. Today the board of Solid Energy has placed the company into 
voluntary administration. This follows months of negotiation with key stakeholders, 
who have agreed to put a proposal to creditors that provides for an orderly sell down of 
assets over the next 2½ years.  
This decision to place the company into voluntary administration was made after it 
became clear that, even with signi ficant operational improvements, the falling 
international coal price means there is no prospect of Solid Energy being in a position to 
repay or refinance its bank debt. Solid Energy owes $320 million in bank debt, some 
falling due in September of 2016, and overall has exposure of close to half a billion 
dollars. As a result of the considerable efforts of its board and management, officials, 
and lenders, Solid Energy is certainly a much more efficient and effective business 
today than it was 2 years ago. But the reality is that there is still no prospect of the 
company being in a position to repay or refinance its debt or access the capital that it 
would require to invest for the future.  
An orderly sales process of Solid Energy gives the best chance that pa rts of the 
business can continue to operate under different ownership in the future. If the creditors 
agree to the proposal, the company will remain solvent during the process and can 
continue to carry on its normal business under its existing board of dir ectors. Payment 
of employees and trade creditors will continue on a business -as-usual basis, and 
customers will continue to have access to coal. Under the terms of the restructure, 
existing Crown indemnities for site rehabilitation costs are being restructured to assist 
the sales process and to provide certainty for affected local authorities. Solid Energy is 
currently exiting and rehabilitating the Pike River mine site. Once it completes this 
process, the land will be returned to the Department of Conserva tion. Through the 
voluntary administration process, Solid Energy remains committed to this work.  
The Government has provided intensive support to the company, in an attempt to 
make it viable in a highly challenging international coal market. Over the past 2 years 
directors, management, banks, and the Government have restructured the company’s 
finances and its operations. This has included commitments of taxpayer support 
totalling more than $250 million. In 2013 the Government negotiated a financial 
restructure package that saw Solid Energy’s banks contribute $75 million in equity to 
the company. The bank also contributed $25 million in equity and offered $130 million 
in low-risk secure loans for the company to use. In 2014 remediation liabilities totalling 
$103 million were transferred from the company to the Crown, which strengthened the 
company’s balance sheet so it could continue trading. 
However, the international coal price has fallen from over US$320 per tonne in 2011 
to around US$85 a tonne this week. Forecast recoveries of the coal price have 
5784 Ministerial Statements 13 Aug 2015 
 
repeatedly failed to eventuate. This low price coupled with the significant levels of debt 
means that the company is no longer sustainable. The Government was prepared to 
provide further support for the company i f there was a reasonable chance it could be 
made viable. We have worked intensively with the company and its bankers on a 
number of options for the company to continue operating, but, unfortunately, none of 
these proved feasible. The Government’s focus wil l continue to be to invest in our core 
business of public services, which we believe is the best way for us to achieve our goal 
of higher living standards for New Zealanders. The Government has been in talks with 
affected councils over the past month, and I have this morning spoken to the mayors of 
these districts to thank them for the constructive way that they have worked through and 
supported this proposal. This voluntary administration offers the best chance for trade 
creditors to be paid and for employees of Solid Energy to continue employment in these 
regions. 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Senior Whip—Labour) : I raise a point of order, Mr Spe aker. I 
would like to draw your attention to Standing Order 356(2), which states pretty clearly 
that if a Minister is going to make a statement, the copy of the statement should, if 
possible, be delivered to the leader of each party before it is made. To m y knowledge, 
that did not happened, and I would like to seek some assurance, first of all from the 
Government, that that will happen in the future when these statements are going to be 
made, as has always been the practice of the House, and secondly, from you, that for 
any consideration that you may be giving after question time to other debate on this 
matter, you will take that into consideration and will not be affected by the fact that the 
Government has made this statement without giving any notice of it to the Opposition. 
Hon TODD McCLAY (Minister for State Owned Enterprises) : My office did 
deliver copies of the statement that I have read in the House, to the best of my 
knowledge, just after 1.30 p.m. today. 
Hon Member: Point of order. 
Mr SPEAKER : Is it in relation to this matter? Let me just rule on this matter. I 
would certainly anticipate that the Government would have sent such copies of this 
statement. That is not a requirement of the Standing Orders but it certainly says that it is 
possible to do so. I can assure the member that decisions that I make subsequent to 
question time are made quite independently of what happens with regard to ministerial 
statements. 
Hon Gerry Brownlee: Mr Speaker— 
Mr SPEAKER: Is it in relation to this matter? 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. Well, yes it is, because the shadow Leader of the House did say that he was 
seeking some assurance. I think the comment that has been made by the Minister 
concerned is reassuring. It is always ou r practice to comply as much as possible, as the 
Standing Orders require of us. I hope that he accepts also that I have tried very much in 
the time that I have been in my current role as Leader of the House to ensure that 
parliamentary procedure is as inclusive as is possible of all those who are a part of it. So 
this is a bit disappointing. It now appears that perhaps some other communication might 
not have occurred that should have. In any event, I hope that the House accepts that we 
are not trying to be in any way obfuscating our responsibilities. Indeed, that is why we 
are having a ministerial statement. 
Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour): This is indeed a very, very sad day, and I 
start by  saying this: I hope Tony Ryall, the former Minister for State Owned 
Enterprises, wherever he may be, is listening very, very— 
Hon Gerry Brownlee: Mr Nasty. 
13 Aug 2015 Ministerial Statements 5785 
 
Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE: —carefully to this. No, no, Mr Brownlee says “Mr 
Nasty”. The Mr Nasty in this piece is a Government that rammed this company into the 
ground—rammed this company into the ground.  
Between 1999 and 2008 Solid Energy was an award- winning export company 
delivering hundreds of millions of dolla rs to the taxpayer. In 2009 the Government’s 
first act by the then Minister for State Owned Enterprises was to write to that company 
and demand more dividends. As a result of that, it took $164 million worth of dividends 
from that company. The Government expected the company, in that letter, which will be 
tabled later today, to ratchet up its debt level, which it did to around, I think, $313 
million. And then when the coal price moved and its own scoping consultants, who 
were in there to scope Solid Energy for sale, reported back in 2009- 10 that the ship was 
heading for the rocks, the Government did nothing. It did absolutely nothing. The alibi 
to the New Zealand people for hundreds of millions of dollars of waste, and for 
probably further hundreds of worker s losing their jobs, is: “Oh! The coal price 
devalued.” 
Well, that is true. The coal price devalued, the markets dried up. Any village idiot on 
that side of the House could have read that in the paper. The question before the New 
Zealand people that the Government has never answered is a simple one: why, when it 
saw that happen, did it not react? Why did it do absolutely nothing—absolutely 
nothing? There was the photo, of course, of Mr English allowing outlandish 
expenditure, opening the lignite path; sexy coal from Mr Brownlee —that is an 
oxymoron—allowing outlandish expenditure, where management spent until it dropped, 
where management and executives, particularly the then chief executive officer, was 
allowed to get a massive golden handshake for sitting at  home. Why did the company 
not react? Other coal companies around the world reacted. 
I have worked in the minerals industry. I have worked there. I know what happens. I 
know what happens when the commodity price moves and companies react within days. 
Coal companies around the world reacted at the same time within days, and they are 
surviving and they are profitable today. These people were derelict in their duty. 
On 5 June 2012 Minister English and then Minister Ryall put the company under

to give some certainty for increases to other welfare payments as well. Interestingly, 
that was not an action taken by the previous Labour Government, along with its partner-
in-arms at the time, the Green Party.

StudyLink assistance will rise to keep up with increasing living costs, and back on 1

$55,027.96.
