NEW ZEALAND FLAG REFERENDUMS BILL 
Third Reading 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) : I move, That the New Zealand 
Flag Referendums Bill be now read a third time. This bill will give New Zealanders the 
opportunity, for the first time ever, to vote on the flag that represents them and their 
country. We made a commitment as a Government, ahead of the last election, and this 
bill delivers on that commitment for a referendum on the flag.  
The first of two postal referendums will soon be held over a 3- week period from late 
November and into December. I just remind the House about the process that was put in 
place, of which this legislation is part. Early on the Government, with the assistance of a 
cross-party group of MPs, set up the Flag Consideration Panel. It was resourced by the 
Government, but in every other respect it has been operating independently and has 
now, through a process of public engagement, particularly through its website, produced 
a long list of 40 flags.  
The members of the cross -party group took quite an interest in the legislation and 
made a number of comments during the Committee stage, questioning whether officials 
had acted properly in the advice that they gave to the  cross-party group. I just want to 
13 Aug 2015 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 5813 
 
put on the record that I have no concerns about the roles that officials have played. 
Cabinet made a decision in October 2014 about the process and the budget for this 
project. The decisions were announced publicly at the  time, and the Cabinet paper and 
minute were made immediately available online. So the process has at all times stressed 
the independence of the Flag Consideration Panel and the transparency of any decision 
making around it. I want to thank the cross-party group for their contribution to this bill.  
Consensus recommendations of the cross -party group are determining the planned 
referendum dates, the preferential voting system used in the first referendum, the 
number of alternative flags on the first referend um voting paper, and the approach to 
regulating referendum advertising. The bill contains the measures required for the 
referendum process to progress. This includes setting out the postal voting processes of 
the two referendums and a promoter statement requirement for those who are publishing 
referendum advertising. The bill also has measures for implementing the new flag if 
voters decide to change the flag, and they are separate and parallel to the work the Flag 
Consideration Panel has been operating.  
The panel has now released a long list of alternative flag designs, and we look 
forward to them accomplishing what must be a difficult task of selecting from those 40 
flags four flags for the purposes of the first referendum. Now that the process for 
underpinning the referendums —the passage of this bill—will be complete, I think that 
the public debate over the flag is likely to rise a few notches in intensity but also in 
relevance to what the flag is about. Up until now it has been dominated, to some extent 
at least, by criticism about the amount of money that is being spent. There has been 
quite a bit of expression of views by people who have every right to oppose any change 
whatsoever and oppose the opportunity for the public to make a choice, which seems a 
bit odd given that that opposition has come mainly from the most populist party in 
Parliament, New Zealand First, which in every other respect believes we should have 
referendums on everything. But apparently on this, when it comes to putting New 
Zealand f irst, New Zealand First members do not believe that New Zealanders are 
capable of exercising a choice about the flag. It is almost as bizarre as the Labour Party 
position, which is to support a change in the flag but oppose a referendum and not vote 
in it.  
Clearly we are heading out of those swirling political waters, fortunately, to the 
sunny uplands where New Zealanders will get to decide what kind of symbol they 
regard stands best for their country and their own sense of identity. I look forward to a 
robust debate in that respect, because, as the Flag Consideration Panel found out, there 
is a wide range of associations that New Zealanders have between the name of their 
country and their flag and the values that they think it represents. I would imagine t hat 
the discussion about the choice of the flag will represent that wide range of associations. 
And then there is the sheer difficulty of understanding the intuitive connections. If you 
think New Zealand is about equality or fairness or freedom, what does that look like on 
a flag? Of course, there will be extensive debate about the balance of representation of 
our history, rich as it is, and our future, aspirational as that is.  
In my capacity as a member of the House I want to acknowledge the role the Prim e 
Minister has played in bringing about this legislation and, in fact, the referendum. 
Leadership is always challenging, and there is no doubt that he has been challenged in 
his desire to see this debate occur. But I have absolutely no doubt that in pushing this 
issue forward he is showing the qualities of leadership and a fundamental belief that 
New Zealanders should have this opportunity. The logic is pretty simple: New 
Zealanders have gained in confidence about their economic capacity and about their 
place in the world. It is a hard- won confidence, through various controversies and 
5814 New Zealand Flag Referendums Bill 13 Aug 2015 
 
recessions and internal political debate, and there is a unique opportunity now for 
people to choose how that confidence should be expressed.  
The Prime Minister was, at the time he raised this issue, almost uniquely aware of the 
need for that opportunity. But the debate that we will see from here, I think, will see 
many New Zealanders grasp that opportunity with two hands and express their views. I 
would counsel the Leader of the Opposition to change his position—he does not usually 
have much difficulty in doing that —on not voting in the referendum. Even if he is 
opposed to change, there is a fundamental legitimacy about a referendum as a way of 
deciding it. Opting out seems to me to be the worst response to the challenge. Get in and 
argue—have a different point of view, try to persuade others. But for a political leader 
to say “Well, I’m not going to participate.” is actually letting down his party and letting 
down his role.  
I look forward to the expression of the will of the people even if the New Zealand 
First Party fears it. I think it will be good for New Zealand to have this debate, and who 
knows—if the alternative is good enough, many of us just might vote for it.
